title: Your Child is Choking, What do You Do? #firstaid. Performing the Heimlich maneuver on a child requires swift and precise action to dislodge an obstructed object from their airway. Follow these steps to administer the Heimlich maneuver on a child: Assess the Situation: Quickly evaluate if the child is genuinely choking. If the child is unable to cough, speak, or breathe, immediate intervention is necessary. Position Yourself: Stand or kneel behind the child, placing one leg between their legs for stability. Reach Around: With your arms, encircle the child's waist. Make a Fist: Form a fist with one hand, placing the thumb side against the child's abdomen, slightly above the navel and below the ribcage. Grasp with Other Hand: Grasp your fist with your other hand. Perform Abdominal Thrusts: Give quick, upward thrusts with both hands, aiming to force the obstructed object out. Continue Until Resolved: Repeat abdominal thrusts until the child can breathe, cough, the object is expelled or the patient loses consciousness. If they do lose consciousness then begin CPR Seek Medical Attention: Even if the child seems fine afterward, it's crucial to seek medical attention to ensure no internal injuries occurred during the maneuver. Put your phone on speaker and quickly move to the next step. Next, place the baby on their back on a firm, flat surface with their head and neck in line and start CPR. For babies under one, place two fingers at the center of their chest, just below the nipple line. Or wrap your arms around the baby and place your two thumbs in the same location on the chest. For those 1 and older, interlace your hands and place them in the center of the chest. For those under one, push down one and a/2 inches or 4 centimeters, and for those one and up, push down 2 inches or 5 centimeters. Allow the chest to rise. Between compressions, perform 30 compressions at a rate of 100 to 1 20 per minute. Compress to the song staying alive to stay on beat. After 30 compressions, give two rescue breaths. Cover the nose and mouth with your mouth, creating a seal. If you can't cover the whole nose and mouth, pinch the nose and cover the mouth. Make sure the Head is in the neutral position for babies and slightly tilted back for kids. To open the airway, give gentle breaths, just enough to make the chest rise and fall. Continue the cycle of 30 compressions and two rescue breaths until help arrives or the child starts breathing. transcript: How to respond if a child or adult is choking. I'm Doctor Yoshi, board certified pediatrician. First, recognize the signs of choking. Someone who is choking might be unable to talk, cough, or breathe, and they might be making the choking sign. Ask if they are choking. If they nod yes or you see the signs, act immediately. Shout for help and have someone call emergency services. If you are alone and have your phone accessible, call emergency services. Put it on speaker and quickly move to the next step. Next, for children 1 year and older and adults, stand or kneel behind them and wrap your arms around their waist. Make a fist with one hand, place it just above the belly button, and then grasp your fist with the other hand. Give quick upward thrusts. These are called abdominal thrusts or the Heimlich maneuver. Continue giving thrusts until the object is expelled or they can breathe, cough, or speak again. If they become unconscious, lay them on the ground and start CPR. title: Paediatric Life Support 🫀🚨👶 Following the rescue breaths, if there are no signs of life or if you are unsure:   - Start good quality chest compressions.  Rate: 100-120 min-1 for both infants and children.   Depth: depress the lower half of the sternum by at least one third of the anterior–posterior dimension of the chest (which is approximately 4 cm for an infant and 5 cm for a child).  - For all children, compress the lower half of the sternum:  - To avoid compressing the upper abdomen, locate the xiphisternum by finding the angle where the lowest ribs join the sternum (breastbone).  Compress the sternum one finger’s breadth above this.  - After each compression, release the pressure completely then repeat at a rate of 100–120 min-1.  Allow the chest to return to its resting position before starting the next compression.  - After 15 compressions, tilt the head, lift the chin, and give rescue breaths.  Continue compressions and breaths in a ratio of 15:2. transcript: Infant CPR is different from adult CPR, and knowing the right steps can make all the difference. Here's what you need to do in an emergency before helping, check your surroundings. Ensure the area is safe for both you and the infant. Gently tap the sole of the infant's foot or their shoulder while calling their name. If there's no response, move to the next step. Place one hand on the infant's forehead and use two fingers to gently lift the chin. Keep the head in a neutral position. Avoid over tilting. Watch the chest for movement. Listen for breathing, and feel for air flow for up to 10 seconds. If the infant is not breathing or only gasping, give five rescue breaths. Create a seal over the infant's mouth and nose with your mouth. Blow gently for about one second, just enough to make the chest rise. Repeat five times. Use two fingers in the center of the infant's chest. Press down about 4 centimeters 1.5 inches at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute. Let the chest fully recoil between compressions. transcript: So most parents and people all together, when they have a baby placed in their arms, they want to hold them in this cradle position. title: Newborn breathing patterns can be a really scary thing for new parents! It seems so different from the way we breathe as adults, but it is normal for them! transcript: How to perform immediate first aid when your child chokes on milk that parents must know. When a baby chokes on milk, many parents panic and quickly lift the baby up to pat them. This is a big mistake because the milk will flow into the baby's lungs, which is extremely dangerous. There is a risk that the baby will suffocate and stop breathing immediately. The correct approach is when you see your baby choking on milk or vomiting, quickly turn the baby on their side, cup your hand and pat the airway between the baby's shoulder blades to let the milk flow out of the mouth. If the baby does not cry, parents should flick the sole of the baby's foot to make them cry, which also helps stimulate breathing. If the baby still has difficulty breathing and turns blue, parents should quickly place the baby face down with the head slightly lower. Use the palm of your hand to firmly pat the baby's back to expel the milk from the respiratory tract. Once the milk flows out, parents should observe the baby's recovery signs. Choking on milk is a very dangerous accident that requires immediate and correct first aid on the spot. Parents, please be attentive and avoid making mistakes.

title: CPR or basic life support is *ESSENTIAL* if your baby (under 1) or child (over 1 to 18 years old) stops breathing. The key is rescue breaths and chest compressions, here are the essential steps to follow from Mini First Aid 1. Check for danger - are they responsive? 2. Call 999 for help.  3. Open the airway and check for breathing for 10 seconds. 4. Give 5 rescue breaths. On a baby, place your mouth over their mouth and nose. On a child, pinch the nose and breathe into mouth. 5. Make sure they are on a hard surface. 8. Return to giving 2 breaths after the compressions and then repeat the pattern until help arrives.  If you’re on your own, and you haven’t got your phone to hand, do a minute of CPR before going to get your phone and making the call. title: When a child is working this hard to breathe, they’re not “just congested.” In pediatrics ER, one of the first signs I pay attention to is work of breathing — how much effort their tiny body is using just to pull air in. title: Would you know what to do if your baby started choking? 🛑 It’s one of the scariest moments a parent can face, but staying calm and knowing the right technique can save a life. At Wellmart Health Solutions, we’re committed to making sure you're prepared. In this video, we together with Princess from Save a Life Foundation demonstrate the 5-and-5 method recommended for infants under age 1: 🖐️ The Steps to Remember: 1. Check the airway: If the baby is coughing strongly or crying, let them try to cough it out. If they can’t breathe, cough, or make sound—act immediately. 2. 5 Back Blows: Rest the baby face-down on your forearm (supported by your thigh) and give 5 firm heel-of-hand blows between the shoulder blades. 3. 5 Chest Thrusts: Turn the baby over and use two fingers to deliver 5 quick thrusts to the center of the chest (similar to CPR compressions, but slower). 4. Repeat: Continue the cycle until the object is cleared or the baby becomes unresponsive. ⚠️ Pro-Tip: Always keep the baby’s head lower than their chest to let gravity help move the object out. Avoid "blind finger sweeps," as you might accidentally push the object deeper. Save this video to your "Safety" folder and share it with your inner circle, nannies, grandparents, and friends. Let’s keep our little ones safe together. #WellmartHealth #BabySafety #ChokingRelief #FirstAidTips #ParentingHacks

title: 🚨 How to Use an AED – Adult & Paediatric Guide 🚨 An AED (Automated External Defibrillator) is a life-saving medical device made for everyone to use whether trained or untrained. title: CPR techniques vary by age. For infants (0-1 year): · Use two fingers for chest compressions if alone, or two thumbs with hands encircling the chest if with another rescuer. · Compress about 1.5 inches deep, 100–120 times per minute. · For breaths, cover the infant's nose and mouth with your mouth to make a seal. For children (1 year to puberty): · Use one or two hands for chest compressions. · Compress about 2 inches deep, 100–120 times per minute. · For breaths, tilt the head back, pinch the nose, and seal your mouth over theirs. For adults: · Use two hands for chest compressions. · Compress at least 2 inches deep, 100–120 times per minute. · For breaths, tilt the head back, pinch the nose, and give two breaths after every 30 compressions. In all cases: 1. Call emergency services immediately. 2. Start with compressions first (C-A-B sequence). 3. If unsure or untrained, do compression-only CPR—push hard and fast in the center of the chest and don’t stop. transcript: Ever wondered how CPR is different for a child? The process starts by checking if the child is responsive. If there's no movement and no normal breathing, you call for help immediately and begin CPR. Place two fingers in the center of the child's chest and push down about one third the depth of the chest using smooth, steady compressions at a rate of 100 to 120 per minute. The force is firm enough to pump blood, but gentler than adult CPR. After 30 compressions, give two rescue breaths. Slightly tilt the head back, lift the chin and cover the child's mouth with yours. Give a soft breath, just enough to make the chest rise, not a full adult breath. Then go straight back to compressions. Continue cycles of 30 compressions and two breaths until help arrives or the child starts breathing on their own. That's how child CPR works. The same life saving technique adjusted with the right pressure and breath for a smaller, delicate body.

title: 📷 NEW technique for delivering chest compressions during baby CPR 📷 Towards the end of last year, the Resuscitation Council UK released new guidelines for best practise in resuscitation, which included some recommended changes to the way we deliver chest compressions and chest thrusts to babies. A child choking is every parent’s worst nightmare - and I’m so grateful for @mikethesituation candor in sharing this moment, to help ALL parents.  A couple of quick things to note:  1. The @american_heart association does NOT recommend back blows for children/toddlers 1 and up (ie any child that can stand). They advise going straight to abdominal thrusts (what we used to refer to as “the Heimlich”). This can be confusing to parents, because other associations (such as the @americanredcross) DO recommend a combination of 5 back blows and then 5 abdominal thrusts. SO - SIMPLEST version: go straight to abdominal thrusts. If someone has medical training (and can tell when a child is still moving air) or training via the American Red Cross, they can do 5 back blows while the child is still moving some air (this is what I'd likely do on my own child). But, as soon as there's complete lack of air movement, switch to abdominal thrusts. 2. If you ARE doing back blows (ie in an infant or if you’re trained via the red cross), then this is not the way to do them. You need to use GRAVITY and FIRMNESS. (watch video while I explain).  3. No major medical group recommends using de-choking devices, including the AHA, Red Cross, ILCOR, and other international groups. While I won’t say DON’T buy it, if you’re a parent who wants to make sure you have EVERYTHING (I get it), I would absolutely say do NOT use it, do NOT waste time trying to find it, and do NOT even consider it, until you’ve done at least 2-3 cycles of REALLY GOOD choking first aid. Then, at most, attempt using one for 2-3 times, and if that doesn’t work, go back to first aid. title: What To Do in Choking? Steps to Manage Choking in an Infant (Below 1 Year) 1️⃣ Recognize the Signs Baby cannot cry, cough, or make sounds Difficulty breathing Lips or face turning bluish Weak or silent cough 2️⃣ Call for Help Ask someone to call emergency medical services immediately while you begin first aid. 3️⃣ Give 5 Back Blows (Most Important step) Place the baby face down on your forearm, supporting the head and neck. Keep the head lower than the chest. Give 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades using the heel of your hand. 4️⃣ Give 5 Chest Thrusts If the object does not come out, turn the baby face up while supporting the head. Place two fingers in the center of the chest (just below the nipple line). Give 5 quick chest thrusts about 4 cm (1.5 inches) deep. 5️⃣ Repeat Continue the cycle of 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts until the object comes out or the baby starts breathing. 6️⃣ If the Baby Becomes Unconscious Place the baby on a firm surface. Start CPR and check the mouth for the object before giving breaths. ❌ What NOT to Do in Infant Choking 1️⃣Do not put your finger blindly in the baby’s mouth (blind finger sweep can push the object deeper). 2️⃣Do not perform abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver) in infants under 1 year. 3️⃣Do not shake the baby to remove the object. 4️⃣Do not try to give water, milk, or food while the baby is choking. 5️⃣Do not delay calling for medical help if choking persists. Sources- Resuscitation Council Guidelines jslookbook on TT The thought of your baby choking is terrifying, but learning Infant Basic Life Support (BLS) is one of the most profound ways you can protect them. Because an infant's airway is incredibly narrow and their coughing reflex lacks the forceful power of an adult's, what might cause a brief coughing fit in an older child can easily become a deadly obstruction in a baby. When a baby's airway is completely blocked, irreversible brain damage from a lack of oxygen can begin in just four to six minutes. Paramedics often cannot arrive within that critical window, making your immediate intervention as a parent the true life-saving measure that keeps your child's brain oxygenated until professional help arrives. A crucial part of this training is learning to instantly recognize the difference between gagging, which is a normal, noisy reflex, and true choking, which is often completely silent. A baby who is truly choking cannot cough, cry, or breathe, and requires immediate, specific physical intervention. Because standard adult Heimlich maneuvers can cause severe internal injuries to a delicate infant, BLS teaches the precise, safe techniques of targeted back blows and gentle chest thrusts performed at a downward angle.  Mastering these specific mechanics replaces panic with empowerment, ensuring you have the confidence to act instantly when seconds count the most. #parenting #basiclifesupport #choking

title: Neonatal stimulation is performed immediately after birth to trigger spontaneous breathing in a newborn whose respiratory system has never been activated outside the womb. During pregnancy the baby receives oxygen directly through the umbilical cord, meaning the lungs have never had to function independently, and the physical stimulus of birth combined with the slap or friction applied to the feet is what signals the nervous system to initiate the first breath. The cry that follows is considered a positive sign because it confirms the airway is open and the lungs are expanding correctly. If stimulation fails to produce a response within the first minute, medical teams move immediately to more intensive intervention since brain damage from oxygen deprivation can begin within minutes of birth. #science #biology #health #medical #nature
transcript: Why do doctors slap babies right after they're born? You might think hitting a Newborn like this could cause harm, but this is actually one of the most important things a doctor can do after birth. The slap is usually applied to the baby's back or chest. The sudden shock of it triggers the baby's first breath by stimulating the nervous system into action. If the baby cries, the lungs are working and air is moving through the airway for the first time. If there's no response, doctors know immediately that something is wrong. It's called neonatal stimulation, and it tells doctors instantly if a Newborn's respiratory system is working properly.

title: DON'T PANIC, ACT FAST! 🍼🚨 ​Choking on milk is every mother's worst nightmare, but knowing exactly what to do in those first 30 seconds can save your baby's life. 🛑 ​The Crucial Rule: If the baby is coughing or gagging—DO NOT intervene. They are clearing their airway naturally. But if they stop breathing or turn blue/pale, every second counts. 🆘 ​The Life-Saving Steps: 1️⃣ 5 BACK BLOWS: Support the jaw, tilt the head down, and strike firmly between the shoulder blades. 2️⃣ 5 CHEST THRUSTS: Flip them over and use two fingers in the center of the chest. 3️⃣ REPEAT: Keep going until the baby cries or breathes normally. ​Pro Tip: If your baby struggles frequently during feeding, consult a lactation specialist for safer positioning. 🤱✨ ​Bottom Line: Save this video now—you hope you’ll never need it, but you’ll be glad you have it. ⚠️❤️ ​ ​#FirstAid  #InfantSafety  #NewMomTips  #ChokingHazards  #BabyHealth

transcript: Hi, I'm Sierra. I'm a board certified Pediatric Nurse Practitioner, mom of three, and I myself have had to give life saving choking first aid to my children twice. So I know how scary this can be, and I want you to be able to confidently do the same. Here are four things to remember when it comes to choking first aid in your baby. First and foremost, know the difference between gagging and choking. These are not the same thing. Agging is loud. It is a protective mechanism of choking. And if we intervene too early, we actually could induce choking. Choking is silent. They are not moving air. They need help from you. Second, if you suspect your baby is choking, do not ever put your finger in their mouth and do a blind finger sweep to try to get the object out. You could actually push the object further back in their mouth and make the situation worse. Third, understand common choking hazards. Understand the characteristics of what makes them choking hazards. So round, hard, firm, rubbery, sticky, gummy. Those things are gonna be choking hazards that we want to complete, we avoid, or remove from the infant. Last, but certainly not least, is knowing how to respond if your baby is truly choking. You're going to calmly but very swiftly lower yourself and your child to the floor or a seated position. You're gonna support the baby's head. You're gonna make sure that their head is Lower than their booty. And you're going to give them five firm back blows with the heel of your hand right between their shoulder blades. And I mean firm. If that didn't work, you're gonna turn them over face up. You're going to look to see if you see the object. If it is not there, you're gonna give them five chest thrusts in the center of their chest with the heel of your hand. If this is an older kiddo, you're gonna make a fist with your hand. You're gonna find their belly button, take your other hand and close it over their fist and give them five abdominal thrusts. You're gonna continue that sequence, five back blows, five chest thrusts or abdominal thrusts, until the object is relieved or until they become unconscious, in which case you need to perform CPR.

It can truly save a life!   A baby in a bib and high chair can still be moved fast in an emergency, but speed is not the first skill. Recognition is. 🚨👶 A lot of caregivers worry, “Would I even get them out in time?” But the bigger issue is knowing what you’re seeing in the first place.   Because gagging and choking are not the same thing. Gagging is often loud, messy, red-faced, watery-eyed, and dramatic. Choking is often silent, still, and scary. That quiet, wide-eyed freeze is what should make you move.   And this is where panic can get people into trouble. When a baby is gagging, sudden grabbing or startling can make things worse. But when a baby is truly choking, this is not the time for light little pats. Back blows need to be firm and purposeful.   The goal isn't to be fearless. It is to be ready. title: You’ve probably seen products like LifeVac or Dechoker marketed as “anti-choking devices” — but here’s what parents should know before relying on them. The American Heart Association and American Academy of Pediatrics reviewed these devices in their 2025 guidelines and found there is currently not enough evidence to recommend for or against their use in children. Most of the available data comes from manufacturer-submitted reports, and these devices have not been proven to work better than standard choking first aid. That means the most important thing you can do is still this: ✔️ Learn CPR ✔️ Learn choking first aid ✔️ Know when to use back blows, chest thrusts, and abdominal thrusts If you choose to keep one of these devices at home: • Never use it instead of standard first aid • Always try recommended choking maneuvers first • Read the instructions before an emergency happens • Make sure you have the correct mask size for your child • Call 911 during any severe choking event And don’t forget prevention matters too: • Cut grapes/hot dogs lengthwise into quarters • Avoid popcorn, nuts, and hard candy for little kids • Keep button batteries, magnets, coins, and small toys out of reach • Avoid latex balloons for young children As a pediatric NP, I never want parents to feel a false sense of security from a product alone. title: Here's why mechanical CPR devices are becoming standard in EMS and hospitals 🫀 Manual chest compressions, while life-saving, are physically demanding. Studies show rescuer fatigue can cause a measurable drop in compression depth and rate within just 1–2 minutes — even among trained providers. Mechanical chest compression devices solve this by delivering: 🫀 Consistent depth and rate, guideline-compliant every time 🫀 Uninterrupted compressions during patient transport 🫀 Reduced rescuer fatigue, allowing the team to focus on other critical interventions This is especially valuable in situations involving long transport times, multiple defibrillation attempts, or extended resuscitation efforts where manual compressions would otherwise need frequent rescuer rotation. The goal isn't to replace human judgment — it's to remove the physical limitations that come with manual CPR, especially when seconds determine the outcome 🩺 ✅ Follow @drdavidabbasi for More Daily Medical Content & Health Tips! 🌴😷 Schedule a consultation in Delray Beach! transcript: In my previous video we spoke about choking in children. Today I'm going to take you through the techniques of how you give back blows, chest thrust, abdominal thrust and mouth motorisation. If your child is choking, has ineffective cough, however they are conscious, you need to deliver back blows. So place your child facing downwards on your lap, support their head. You deliver five blows in between their shoulder blades. Every time you do this, check their mouth to see if the foreign body has come out. You are able to see it and grasp and remove it out if you can see it. If not, you need to now continue to give chest thrust. For the chest thrust, now lay your baby facing upwards with your two fingers, place them on the lower part of their chest and deliver five chest thrust by compressing around 2 to 3 cm. For children more than 1 year of age, you can replace the chest thrust with abdominal thrust. You can either stand behind or kneel behind the child. Wrap your arms around the waist with your fist, closed fist with the thumb facing upwards, place it on their abdomen just above their navel and below their breastbone. Encircle the other hand onto this wrist so that it can give you support and deliver quick thrusts which are upward and inward. Five times. You need to repeat these cycles of back blows, chest thrust or abdominal thrust one after the other. Until the object is expelled out, until your child is conscious. If your child is unconscious, however, you need to do mouth to mouth resuscitation. For the mouth to mouth resuscitation, place the baby on a firm surface, tilt the head to open the airway, establish that there is no breathing. So you look for the breathing movements of the chest. You listen if there are any breathing sounds that you can hear and you feel for the gush of air with any breath. If there's nothing suggestive of breathing, you now seal your lips to the mouth and nose of the baby and breathe steadily for around 1 second. These are called rescue breaths. Give five such rescue breaths to your baby. Soon after this, now you have to deliver chest compressions using your two fingers on the lower part of the chest. You compress 30 times at the depth of 2 to 3 cm. After every 30 compressions, you need to give two rescue breaths. Continue this cycle continuously until you get help. These techniques are extremely important and life-saving measures. Please feel free to reach out to me if you have any further questions or clarifications.

The ARC instructs rescuers to immediately resume CPR, beginning with chest compressions. 🟥 What “No Shock Advised” Means (ARC Standard) The AED has analyzed the heart’s electrical activity.It did not find one of the two shockable rhythms (V‑Fib or pulseless V‑Tach). Therefore, no shock will be delivered. The ARC explicitly states:After the AED delivers a shock, or if no shock is advised, immediately start CPR, beginning with compressions.  Source: https://www.redcross.org/take-a-class/aed/using-an-aed/aed-steps?utm_source=copilot.com 🟦 Why This Happens (Based on AED Analysis) The AED may detect:  Asystole (flatline) Pulseless Electrical Activity (PEA)  A normal or organized rhythm A rhythm that CPR—not a shock—can help improve These are all non‑shockable rhythms, so the AED correctly advises no shock. 🟩 What You Must Do Next (ARC Protocol) Resume CPR immediately — do NOT pause. Keep AED pads attached so the device can continue analyzing every 2 minutes. Follow all voice prompts until EMS arrives. title: What to Do If a Baby Is Choking If an infant under 1 year is choking, do not do the Heimlich. The correct first aid is: 5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts, and repeat. Hold the baby face-down on your forearm, with the head lower than the chest, and give 5 back blows between the shoulder blades. Then turn the baby face-up, keep the head lower than the chest, and give 5 chest thrusts using two fingers in the center of the chest, just below the nipple line. Repeat 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts until the object comes out or the baby can breathe or cry. If the baby becomes unresponsive, call emergency services and begin CPR. #ParentingTips #ParentingAdvice #Pediatrician #PediatricianTips #BabySafety

Luckily on this one it was a false alarm! 👃 Did you know there’s a simple technique that can sometimes remove an object from a child’s nose—without using instruments? Before reaching for forceps or heading to the emergency department, certain smooth objects in a child’s nose may be removed using the “Mother’s Kiss” technique. 💨 Here’s how it works: • Close the unaffected nostril with a finger. • Place your mouth over your child’s mouth, creating a seal. • Give one short, firm puff of air while keeping the other nostril closed. • The burst of air can sometimes push the object out of the blocked nostril. ✅ It can be very effective for smooth objects like beads or small pieces of foam. ❌ It should not be attempted if the object is a button battery, paired magnets, sharp objects, or if your child is having trouble breathing. Those situations require immediate medical evaluation. Sometimes the simplest techniques work the best. 🏠 Des Moines Mobile Medicine & Virtual Care 📞 515-770-1424 🌐 desmoinesmobilemedicine.com

title: I did mine for $60, and feel like new parents, teachers, babysitters, and ANYONE should be CPR/BLS certified #cprcertified#basiclifesupporttraining#anyonecandoit#cprsaveslives
transcript: Do you have three hours and can scramble up somewhere around $100? You really should be CPR certified. CPR certified and BLS certified, like basic life support certified, AED certified, they all come in the same class. Because even if you're not working in healthcare, knowing how to do CPR and knowing how to do basic life support like the Heimlich maneuver, back blows on babies to dislodge food from the throat, all of those things are very important. Imagine you're a babysitter or a new parent and a child starts choking on food. Or imagine you're at a restaurant and someone starts choking. Imagine you're shopping through the mall and somebody falls out and they go into cardiac arrest. You don't need to be the perfect Superman in that moment. You might be scared, shocked and even freeze up for a second feeling like you don't know what to do. But the thing that will take you out of that freeze response is knowing that you have the knowledge and the training and the ability to do something, to do anything. If you're not a health care provider, the CPR doesn't have to be the most quality CPR you've ever done in your entire life. But if you are in a room of 15 people and you're the only person there that knows how to do CPR or that has had CPR training, you should get on in there and do it. If you're babysitting in the baby is Choking, knowing that you have to deliver five strong back blows at an angle can help save that baby's life versus maybe the initial idea of just like digging your hand in its mouth, trying to see what's in there. Understanding that CPR and BLS can be used in a variety of situations and scenarios is key. You can go on the American Heart Association website or the American Red Cross website and look up CPR classes near me. It should bring up a drop down of zip codes and a list of classes that are in your area. And the number should range from like 60 to 100 dollars. The quality of the class isn't impacted by the cost of the class. But if you have any spare time and the ability to participate in these classes, I think everybody, regardless of their work status, should be CPR and BLS certified.

title: Here is exactly what to do if your baby is choking.  5 black blows. 5 chest thrusts. Alternate until obstruction clears or the child goes unconscious. transcript: Your baby is choking. They are not moving any air. They are unable to breathe. They are completely silent and they are not coughing or crying. What are you going to do about it? You are going to remove them from their high chair, place them over your arm like so with a bit of gravity. You're gonna give them five back blows, one, two, three, 4, 5. If they are still choking, you are going to turn them over onto their back. You are going to do five chest thrusts, one, two, three, 4, 5. transcript: If your baby always seems to have noisy breathing, especially during feeding or while lying on their back, one possible cause is something called laryngomalacia. It's the most common cause of noisy breathing in young infants and happens because the tissue just above the vocal cords is more soft than usual. When the baby breathes in, that tissue can briefly fall inward, partially narrowing the airway and creating that high pitch sound. Because breathing takes more effort, some babies also have trouble feeding, tire easily during feeds, or don't gain weight as expected. The good news is that most cases are mild and improve on their own as the airway grows stronger, usually by 12 to 18 months of age. Babies with more severe symptoms may need additional treatment or in some cases, surgery. If your baby has noisy breathing, trouble feeding, poor weight gain, pauses in breathing, or bluish color around the lips, it is important to let your pediatrician know. title: Baby CPR is one of those skills you hope you’ll never need, but you’ll be so grateful you know if you ever do. 🤍 If a baby is unresponsive and not breathing normally: 👣 TAP and check for a response 📞 CALL for help and emergency medical services 🫀 Give 30 chest compressions at 100–120 compressions per minute 💨 Give 2 gentle breaths 🔁 Continue 30 compressions + 2 breaths until help arrives or baby starts breathing normally ⚠️ The CPR demonstration in this video has been sped up. Do not use the video speed to guide your compression rate. Save the CPR card at the end to keep on your phone, and share this with another parent, grandparent or caregiver. 🤍 Knowing what to do before an emergency happens can make all the difference. Save it. Share it. Learn it. #babycpr #infantcpr #BabySafety #firstaid

transcript: The most important lifesaving skill that every parent needs to know is how to handle choking. Knowing the skill is not optional if you have kids, because the only person who's gonna be able to save your child's life if they're actually choking is the person within arms reach of that child. And most of the time, that is you. I became passionate about this topic when I had to save my own child's life when she was two. My disclaimer is that this video is not a substitute for taking a formal, approved C P R. Course, but it is a pretty good introduction of what you need to know. My assistant, Phil, is going to help us through this process. There are two things to not do and two things to do if your child is choking. So let's start with what not to do. First thing not to do is if your child is making noise, you do not intervene. Real choking noise stops. If your child is making sound, you do nothing and watch. The second thing not to do is you never blind sweep a child's mouth. The reason why is a child's airway is shaped like a funnel and not a cylinder. You can accidentally push a foreign object or food further in and jam it and make it harder to get out. So do not blind sweep your child's mouth. The two things to do if you need to intervene, you do back Blows and abdominal thrusts. If you have a toddler, meaning a child that walks. Back blows look like this. Hold the child over, and you hit them between the shoulder blades as hard as you can, like you're trying to hurt them. Five back blows followed by abdominal thrusts. A fist below the belly button and push in hard. That's for a toddler. For an infant, back blows are holding your infant head down. Back blows, five. Then you turn them over. Adopt chest thrusts. In an infant, two fingers on the breastbone, five times hard. And that is how you're going to save your child's life if they're choking. title: ⚠️ Household choking hazards you might be missing… We all know to keep small objects away from babies and toddlers, but it’s often the everyday things around the house that are easiest to overlook 👀 🖊️ Pen lids – small enough to end up straight in their mouth 🎀 Hair clips & bobbles – easily dropped on floors or left within reach 🐾 Pet food – pieces can be the perfect size and shape to become a choking hazard 🥤 Bottle lids – something we often leave lying around without thinking 🔋 Batteries – small batteries can be a choking hazard, and button/coin batteries are especially dangerous if swallowed as they can cause severe internal injury. 🧸 Older children’s toys – small parts that are safe for an older sibling may not be safe for a baby or toddler 🔵 Blu Tack – another small item that can easily find its way into little mouths Once babies are mobile, EVERYTHING seems to go in their mouth 😅 A quick floor-level check around the house can help you spot things you might otherwise miss. Save this as a reminder and send it to another parent who might find it useful 🤍 #BabySafety #ToddlerSafety #ChokingHazards #ParentingTips #BabyProofing

transcript: We've had so many new followers recently, so let's do an updated video. What is DMI? What you're seeing is a technique called DMI, which stands for Dynamic Movement intervention. In very simple terms, DMI Gives the child's body a movement problem to solve. Essentially, gravity and changes in position challenge the child's muscles to switch on for posture, balance, and movement. Instead of the therapist passively doing the work for the child. The goal of all of these exercises are to encourage the child's active movement and participation. DMI Exercises provide lots of vestibular and proprioceptive information. These are our sensory systems that help us know where our body is in space. With all these exercises, the brain now has to take all of the sensory information coming in and organise a response to help keep themselves upright. The goal with DMI is for responses that initially require a lot of effort and support from the therapist to become more efficient and more automatic so that the child can then incorporate it in their everyday lives. DMI Was primarily designed for children with significant motor delays, often due to medical complexity from a genetic or a neurological condition, for example. What makes DMI Different from traditional therapy is that it's a very hands on technique. A physical therapist can place emphasis on active responses to carefully graded movement challenges and this allows a child to Eventually get stronger over time and do those same responses with their own body versus the PT passively guiding them through the same movements over and over. As a child gains more independence, the therapist can then progress the exercises and make them more challenging, and in this way, DMI Aims to stimulate neuroplasticity. For children with significant delays or complex medical histories, movement doesn't always come easily, and they may not get the opportunity to explore and learn through movement like other children. This is why DMI Is so powerful for these children. We meet the child exactly where they are, give the body the right amount of challenge, and create movement opportunities that they may not have been able to have on their own!

Call for emergency help 	•	If someone is nearby, ask them to call emergency services and get an AED. 	•	If you are alone, begin CPR first according to your local emergency guidance. 	4.	Give chest compressions 	•	Place 2 fingers in the center of the baby’s chest, just below the nipple line. 	•	Compress about one-third of the chest depth (approximately 4 cm). 	•	Rate: 100–120 compressions per minute. 	•	Allow the chest to fully recoil after each compression. 	5.	Give 2 rescue breaths 	•	Cover the baby’s mouth and nose with your mouth. 	•	Give 2 gentle breaths, just enough to make the chest visibly rise. 	6.	Continue 30:2 	•	30 compressions → 2 breaths, repeatedly. 	•	If two trained rescuers are providing CPR, use 15 compressions : 2 breaths. 	7.	Use an AED as soon as available 	•	Use pediatric/infant pads if available; otherwise follow the AED’s instructions.@__Abimbola 💋💞

title: This is one of the most important differences between pediatric and adult resuscitation. Pediatric bradycardia is frequently caused by **hypoxemia and respiratory failure**. That's why the initial priorities include: • Opening the airway • Providing oxygen • Supporting effective ventilation But what if the heart rate remains **below 60 beats per minute** and the child still has signs of cardiopulmonary compromise? That's when PALS directs you to begin **chest compressions, even when a pulse is still present.** Here's the physiology behind it: **Cardiac Output = Heart Rate × Stroke Volume** Infants, especially neonates and young infants, have a more limited ability to increase stroke volume compared with adults. That makes their cardiac output much more dependent on heart rate. So when the heart rate becomes severely slow, cardiac output can fall quickly. And here's the important part: A palpable pulse does NOT automatically mean perfusion is adequate. A child may still have a pulse but not have enough cardiac output to maintain adequate: • Coronary perfusion • Cerebral perfusion • End organ oxygen delivery But don't reduce this to: Heart rate below 60 = CPR. Three things matter: 1. The heart rate is below 60 beats per minute 2. Cardiopulmonary compromise is present 3. The bradycardia persists **despite effective ventilation with oxygen** And that last part matters. If oxygenation and ventilation are not effective, correcting the respiratory problem is critical because **hypoxemia may be what is driving the bradycardia in the first place.** Another high yield distinction: Atropine is NOT the universal first medication for pediatric bradycardia. Atropine is considered when increased vagal tone or primary AV block is suspected. The treatment pathway depends on the cause. The monitor tells you the rate. Perfusion tells you whether that rate is producing enough cardiac output. transcript: What to do if your baby is choking. I'm Dr. Yoshi, board certified pediatrician. I've gotten a ton of messages asking for a demonstration of what to do if your baby is choking, so here are the steps. First, recognize the signs. If a baby is choking, they might not be able to cry or cough. They might have difficulty breathing, and their skin might turn blue, especially around the lips and face. If you see these signs, act quickly but calmly. First, yell for help and have somebody call emergency services. If you are alone and have your phone accessible, call emergency services, put it on speaker, and quickly move to the next step. Next, for babies under one, support their head and their jaw with your hand. Place them on your forearm, facing down, and make sure that their head is below their chest. Give up to five firm back blows between the baby's shoulder blades with the heel of your hand. If the object isn't dislodged, turn the baby over onto their back, supporting them with your arm. Make sure their head is still below their chest, and perform.

title: Abdominal thrusts and back blows can be life-saving when someone is choking and cannot breathe, speak, or cough effectively. The key is knowing when and how to act rather than waiting for the obstruction to clear on its own. * Encourage effective coughing if the person can still cough or speak. * If the person has a severe airway obstruction, give 5 firm back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts, alternating until the object comes out or the person becomes unresponsive. * For a pregnant person or someone around whom you cannot get your arms, use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts. * If the person becomes unresponsive, lower them to the ground, call 911/get an AED, and begin CPR. Look in the mouth for an object when opening the airway, but don’t perform a blind finger sweep. For a choking emergency, acting quickly matters because a completely blocked airway can lead to unconsciousness and cardiac arrest within minutes.#cpr #savinglives #womenover50 #friendships #funnyskits

transcript: If you have to use an AED on a small child, things change because standard defibrillators deliver a massive jolt of electricity meant for a fully grown adult heart. So what do you do if a kid under 8 years old goes into cardiac arrest? Ideally, you swap in a smaller set of pediatric pads or you press the pediatric setting on the device. This physically tells the machine to lower the shock energy. But most public AED kits only have adult pads and searching for alternatives wastes critical seconds. The emergency work around you use the adult pads anyway. An immediate shock is always better than delaying care for perfect equipment. But there's one strict rule when putting those oversized adult pads on a small frame, they have to be placed so their edges never touch each other. And that young child who collapsed in cardiac arrest from the very beginning, they successfully receive the life saving shock that they urgently need without any dangerous pad overlap.

title: When To Actually Apply AED Pads #Defibrillator #lifesavingdevice #safetytips #SaveALife #workplacewellness #hearthealth #aedprofessionals #minnesotaaedlaws #aedoperations #rescueready #workplacesafetyawareness #pediatrician #pediatrics #bleedingcontrol #aedlaws #emergencypreparedness #workplacesafety #firstaidkit #choking #cpr
transcript: Someone collapses, you grab the AED, but a terrifying thought freezes you. What if I shock a healthy heart? Here are the exact rules for applying the pads. First, the machine decides, not you. An AED is just a rhythm analyzer. If the heart is beating normally or totally flatlined, it physically won't let you deliver a charge. Next, skip the pulse check in a panic. Amateurs get this wrong and it delays chest compressions. The only requirement? They are unresponsive and not breathing normally. Third, if they are unresponsive but making irregular snoring or gasping sounds, attach the pads immediately. This reflex, called agonal respiration, comes from an oxygen starved brain. Treat it as cardiac arrest. Finally, never attach an AED to a conscious person. If they are awake and sweating, they need an ambulance for a heart attack, not a defibrillator. Because the machine prevents unnecessary shocks, the only wrong choice in an unresponsive emergency is hesitating to use it.

transcript: Hearing strange breathing sounds from your baby. It might be laryngomalacia. I'm Doctor Yoshi, board certified pediatrician. Lingual malacia is a condition where the soft tissues of the throat are floppy and fall over the airway slightly when your baby inhales. It's the most common cause of noisy breathing in infants. How can you tell it's lingual malacia? The key sign is that the noise gets louder when they're on their back, feeding or crying. This might sound scary, but it's usually not serious and tends to get better over time. In fact, most babies grow out of it by 18 to 24 months. In most cases, no treatment is needed, just regular checkups to monitor your baby's breathing. However, if your baby is having trouble feeding or gaining weight, the breathing affects their sleep. Noisy breathing is increasing in frequency, or if your baby starts to have more rapid breathing, it's important to see your pediatrician.

title: A child who becomes short of breath, struggles to breathe, or cannot properly catch their breath while crying should be taken seriously. First, stay calm and keep the child as comfortable as possible. Stop activities and allow them to sit upright or remain in the position in which breathing is easiest. 👀 Watch for warning signs such as: • Very fast or difficult breathing • Ribs or the skin between the ribs pulling inward • Noisy breathing, wheezing, or a harsh sound when breathing in • Blue, gray, or unusually pale lips or face • Difficulty speaking, crying, or making normal sounds • Extreme sleepiness, confusion, or loss of consciousness 🚨 If the child is struggling to breathe, turning blue/gray, becoming unresponsive, or suddenly cannot breathe normally, call your local emergency medical service immediately. Do not force to drink, and don’t put anything into the child’s mouth unless you’re performing an appropriate first-aid procedure. If the episode happens repeatedly—even if the child appears normal afterward—contact a pediatrician to determine the underlying cause. Breathing difficulty in a child can have many causes, including asthma, infection, allergic reactions, airway obstruction, or other conditions. The cause cannot be diagnosed from crying alone. When a child is struggling to breathe, don’t wait for the episode to “pass” if serious warning signs are present. USMLE Step 2 Pediatrics Q135 Correct Answer: D. Rigid bronchoscopy This child has foreign body aspiration, most likely involving the right main bronchus. Key clues: Sudden coughing while playing, unilateral decreased breath sounds, localized expiratory wheezing, and air trapping on expiratory chest x-ray. A partially obstructing foreign body creates a ball-valve effect: air enters during inspiration but cannot fully escape during expiration, causing unilateral hyperinflation. A. CT chest CT can identify radiolucent foreign bodies but is unnecessary when clinical findings strongly suggest aspiration. Bronchoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic. B. Inhaled albuterol Albuterol treats reversible bronchospasm, such as asthma, which typically causes diffuse wheezing. Focal wheezing with unilateral air trapping suggests mechanical obstruction. C. Oral dexamethasone Dexamethasone treats croup, which presents with a barking cough, inspiratory stridor, and often a preceding viral illness. It cannot remove an aspirated object. D. Rigid bronchoscopy Directly visualizes and removes the foreign body while allowing airway control. It is the preferred intervention for suspected pediatric airway foreign bodies. E. Observation Normal oxygen saturation and absence of respiratory distress do not exclude aspiration. Delayed removal increases the risk of persistent obstruction, postobstructive pneumonia, and atelectasis.

Newborn resuscitation: “Newborn resuscitation is a series of emergency steps used to help a newborn who is not breathing properly or has a low heart rate after birth.”3–4 Basic Steps: Position the baby – Place the newborn on a firm, warm surface and keep the head in a neutral/slightly extended position. Clear the airway – If needed, clear secretions from the mouth and nose. Provide ventilation – If the baby is not breathing adequately, give positive-pressure ventilation (PPV) using a bag and mask. Chest compressions – If the heart rate remains very low despite effective ventilation, start chest compressions using the two-thumb technique.

title: Not all CPR techniques are the same—especially when it comes to infants. 👶 In this video, we break down three key approaches to infant CPR and when each may be used: 1. Two-Finger Technique — Single Rescuer    Ideal when you are performing CPR alone. This technique uses the pads of two fingers to deliver chest compressions at the center of the infant’s chest, just below the nipple line. 2. Two-Thumb Encircling Hands Technique — Two or More Rescuers    When a second rescuer is available, this technique allows the rescuer to encircle the infant’s chest with both hands and use their thumbs to deliver controlled chest compressions. It can provide better control of compression depth and reduce rescuer fatigue. 3. Heel of One Hand Technique    This technique may sometimes be considered depending on the infant’s size and physical development, although it is less commonly used for very small infants. So, which technique should you use? If you are the only rescuer, the two-finger technique is commonly used. When two or more rescuers are available, the two-thumb encircling hands technique may be preferred because it allows for more consistent and controlled compressions. In an emergency, knowing the correct technique can make all the difference. title: Paediatric Basic Life Support - 2021 key points from the UK Resus
description:
The 2021 UK Resuscitation Council guidelines have added a few key points about Paediatric basic life support.  In the paediatric basic life support sequence, rescuers should perform an assessment for signs of life, like circulation, simultaneously with breathing assessment and during the delivery of rescue breaths.  If there are no signs of life, chest compressions should be started immediately after rescue breaths have been delivered.

There is an emphasis on rescuers using mobile phones with speaker function to facilitate bystander access to dispatcher guided cardiopulmonary resuscitation known as CPR and to summon emergency medical services (EMS) without leaving the child or infant.

In certain situations, such as when the child or infant is breathing spontaneously but requires airway management or when the child has a traumatic injury, the recovery position is not recommended. In these circumstances:

Keep the patient flat, maintain an open airway by either continued head tilt and chin lift or jaw thrust.

For trauma victims, leave the child or infant lying flat and open and maintain the airway using a jaw thrust, taking care to avoid spinal movement.

High-quality CPR is emphasised in the guidelines which are obtained by:

A chest compression depth is at least one third the anterior-posterior diameter of the chest, or by 4 cm for the infant and 5 cm for the child.

The chest compression pauses are minimised so that 80% or more of the CPR cycle is comprised of chest compressions chest at a  rate of 100 to 120 per min. And finally by allowing full recoil of the chest after each chest compression.

title: How to do CPR on an Adult (Ages 12 and Older)
description:
http://www.cincinnatichildrens.org/cpr-adults 
Cincinnati Children's Demonstrates Adult CPR (Ages 12 and Older).

Transcript:
You Arrive on the Scene

Check the scene for safety. Check the victim for consciousness. Gently tap the shoulder and shout.

No Response

Call 911 immediately.

If the adult is on his or her stomach, turn the person over onto his or her back. The person should be lying on a hard flat surface.

Check for Breathing and Signs of Life

Watch the chest for any normal movement. Look for signs of life and breathing for no more than 10 seconds. 

No Breathing or Signs of Life

Begin CPR

a. Position the heel of one hand on the center of the adult’s chest.  Place your other hand on top.

b. With your elbows locked and arms straight, lean over the adult and compress the chest 2 inches in depth 30 times.

c. After 30 compressions, give breaths by tilting the head back, lifting the chin and pinching the nose. Give two slow and gentle breaths. The chest should rise with each breath.

d. Continue with 30 compressions / two breaths, 30 compressions / two breaths, etc. 

Continue CPR until another rescuer takes over, you see signs of life or help arrives.

title: 3i: BLS for Children/Infants (2026)
description:
In this video, we will discuss basic life support for children and infants.

BLS for children and infants also focuses on doing several tasks simultaneously. In many situations, more than one person is available to do CPR.

This simultaneous and choreographed method includes performing chest compressions, managing the airway, delivering rescue breaths, and using the AED, all as a team. By coordinating efforts, a team of rescuers can save valuable seconds when time lost equals damage to the heart and brain.

ONE-RESCUER BLS/CPR FOR CHILDREN (AGE 1 TO PUBERTY)
Be Safe
• Move the child out of traffic or any unsafe situation.
• Move the child out of water and dry the child. (Drowning children should be removed from the water and dried off; they should also be removed from standing water, such as puddles, pools, gutters, etc.)
• Be sure you do not become injured yourself.

Assess the Child
• Tap hard on their shoulder and talk to them loudly, saying their name.
• Check to see if the child is breathing while simultaneously checking their carotid pulse. (Agonal breathing, which is occasional gasping and is ineffective, does not count as breathing.)
• Keep in mind not to waste time trying to feel for a pulse; feel for at least 5 seconds but no more than 10 seconds. If you are not sure you feel a pulse, begin CPR with a cycle of 30 chest compressions and two breaths.

Call EMS
• Send someone for help and to get an AED.
• If alone, shout for help while assessing for breathing and pulse. (The ILCOR emphasizes that cell phones are available everywhere now and most have a built-in speakerphone. Call for help without leaving the child.)
• If no one answers and you do not have a cell phone available, perform 2 minutes of CPR before taking a moment to find help.

CPR
• Begin CPR with chest compressions and delivering breaths in a ratio of 30:2.
Defibrillate
• Attach the AED when it becomes available. Use pediatric pads for children under the age of 8 and less than 55 pounds (25 kg).
• Listen to the AED and perform the steps as directed.

title: What to Do If an Adult or Child Is Choking?
description:
Witnessing someone choking can be a scary experience, but jumping into action can mean the difference between life and death. More often than not, choking happens when someone gets a piece of food (or another small object) stuck in their windpipe. 

Abdominal Thrusts, also referred to as the Heimlich maneuver, can help you remove this foreign object and encourage the person to start breathing again. But how do you perform this life-saving action?

Administer abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver). The Heimlich maneuver is an emergency technique that is only to be used on adults or children older than 1 year of age. Do not use the Heimlich maneuver on children under 1 year old.

Steps:
1. Stand behind the choking victim.
2. Put your arms around his waist and lean him forward.[9]
3. Make a fist with your hand and place it directly above the person's navel (belly button) but below the breastbone.
4. Put your other hand on top of your first, then thrust both hands backwards into their stomach with a hard, upward movement.
5. Do this thrusting action up to five times. Check after each thrust to see if the blockage is gone. 
6. Begin CPR if the victim loses consciousness.

title: PEDIATRIC CPR Explained Simply
description:
Pass School & NREMT Exams, Go Here: https://www.prepareforems.com

Get my EKG/12-Lead EKG Masterclass: https://www.ekgforems.com

Pediatric Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) according to the American Heart Association (AHA) involves specific steps tailored to infants and children up to puberty. The process begins with ensuring the scene is safe for both the rescuer and the patient. Once safety is confirmed, check the child’s responsiveness by gently tapping and shouting. For infants, you should tap the bottom of the foot. If there is no response, activate the emergency response system. If you are alone with a child or infant and there is no response, perform CPR for 2 minutes before leaving to call emergency services. If another person is present, have them call emergency services immediately.

Next, open the airway using the head-tilt-chin-lift technique. Be careful with the amount of tilt, especially in infants. Check for breathing and a pulse for no more than 10 seconds. For infants, check the brachial pulse, and for children, check the carotid or femoral pulse. 

For chest compressions in infants (under 1 year), use two fingers in the center of the chest, just below the nipple line, pressing to a depth of at least 1.5 inches (4 cm) at a rate of 100-120 compressions per minute. For children (1 year to puberty), use one or two hands (depending on the size of the child) on the lower half of the breastbone, pressing to a depth of at least 2 inches (5 cm), but not more than 2.4 inches (6 cm), at the same rate of 100-120 compressions per minute.

After compressions, provide rescue breaths. For both infants and children, give 2 breaths after every 30 compressions (or 15:2 if two rescuers are present). Each breath should last about 1 second and make the chest rise visibly. Use an Automated External Defibrillator (AED) as soon as it is available. For infants and children under 8 years, use pediatric pads if available. If not, use adult pads, placing them so they do not touch each other. Follow the AED prompts and resume CPR immediately after each shock, continuing until the child shows signs of life or emergency medical personnel take over.

Continue cycles of 30 compressions and 2 breaths (or 15:2 if two rescuers are present) until the child shows signs of life, an AED is ready to use, or professional help arrives. These steps ensure that CPR provided to pediatric patients follows the AHA's guidelines for optimal outcomes.

title: Finger Positions to perform chest compressions during neonatal resuscitation
description:
The Neonatal Life Support Consensus on Science With Treatment Recommendations states that chest compressions be performed preferably with the 2-thumb encircling technique. The aim of this study was to compare the hemodynamic effects of four different finger positions during chest compressions in a piglet model of neonatal asphyxia. Methods: Seven asphyxiated post-transitional piglets were randomized to chest compressions with 2-thumb-, 2-finger-, knocking-fingers-, and over-the-head 2-thumb-techniques for one minute at each technique. Chest compressions superimposed with sustained inflations were performed manually. 
Conclusion: The 2-thumb-technique and the over-the-head 2-thumb-technique resulted in improved slope rises of carotid blood flow and dp/dtmin during chest compression.

description:
If a baby is choking, they won’t be able to cry, cough or breathe. Here's what you need to do if a baby is choking...
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
VIDEO TRANSCRIPT:

If a  baby is choking, they won’t be able to cry, cough or breathe. This is what to do if a baby is choking:
• Hold them face down on your thigh with their head downwards.
• Support their head with your hand.
• Hit them firmly on their back between their shoulder blades. These are called back blows. 
• Do this 5 times.
• Check if anything’s come out. If this has worked, the obstruction should have come out.
• If it hasn’t worked, turn the baby over so they are face up.
• Put two fingers in the middle of their chest – in line with their nipples.
• Push sharply down 5 times – this is called a chest thrust. The aim is to squeeze the air out of the baby’s lungs to dislodge the obstruction.
• Check their mouth to see if it’s worked.
• If it hasn’t worked call the emergency services.

While waiting for help to arrive keep repeating the cycle of 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts until help comes or the obstruction comes out. If the baby loses consciousness or become unresponsive at any stage, check their airway and give them CPR if they stop breathing.

transcript: If after performing a primary survey, you find a child who is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call for help. Ask someone to phone 999 or 112, and ask them to bring an AED if one is available, while you begin CPR immediately. If you're by yourself and do not have a speakerphone, start CPR with five initial rescue breaths, then 30 chest compressions and 2 rescue breaths for one minute before calling for help. To give rescue breaths, open the airway by tilting the head back with one hand on the forehead and two fingers under the chin. Pick out any obstructions from their mouth to clear the airway only if you can clearly see something. Keeping the head in this position, pinch the soft part of the nose. Allow the mouth to fall open. Take a deep breath and seal your mouth around theirs. Blow steadily into their mouth, giving a rescue breath in about one second. The chest will rise. Remove your mouth from theirs and watch their chest fall. Give them five initial rescue breaths at about one breath per second, like this. To do chest compressions, kneel down by child, beside their chest. Place only one hand on the centre of the chest. Lean over the child with your arms straight and press down vertically one-third of its depth. Release the pressure. Allow the chest to come back up without removing your hand from the chest. Repeat this to give 30 chest compressions at a rate of 100 to 120 beats per minute. This is quite fast and to help you, you can sing Nellie the Elephant, which can help you to keep up with the pace. After thirty chest compressions, open the airway and give them a further two rescue breaths. Continue to alternate between thirty chest compressions and two rescue breaths until help arrives. If you're on your own and don't have a speakerphone, stop after one minute and call 999 or 112 for emergency help If a mobile phone is not available and you have to move to get a telephone, take the child with you if you are able. Do not leave the child to look for an AED - the emergency services will bring one with them. If there is someone there who can help, if they brought an AED, ask them to turn it on and follow instructions while you continue CPR. If they can help you perform CPR, you can swap over every one to two minutes with minimal interruptions to chest compressions. Continue CPR until emergency help arrives and takes over, the child starts to show signs of becoming responsive, they start breathing normally or opening their eyes, or you become too exhausted to continue. If they do start breathing normally again, put them in the recovery position. So remember: if you come across a child that's unresponsive and not breathing normally, call for help. Tell a helper to call 999 or 112 straightaway and ask them to bring an AED. Give five initial rescue breaths Then thirty chest compressions followed by two rescue breaths. Continue giving 30 chest compressions to 2 rescue breaths until help arrives, or the child starts to breathe. And that's how we perform CPR on a child. This video provides a clear and concise guide to the pediatric cardiac arrest algorithm for single rescuers. Learn the essential steps to take in this critical situation, from assessing the child's responsiveness to administering CPR and using an AED:
◾ Scene Safety: Always ensure the scene is safe before approaching the child.
◾ Responsiveness and Pulse Check: Quickly assess the child's responsiveness and check for a pulse.
◾ Emergency Breaths: If the child is unresponsive and not breathing or only gasping, provide rescue breaths.
◾ Witnessed Collapse: If you witnessed the collapse, immediately prepare the AED, check for a shockable rhythm, and shock if possible.
Unwitnessed Collapse: If the collapse was not witnessed, perform CPR before using the AED.
◾ Non-Shockable Rhythm: If the AED advises no shock, continue CPR and wait for help to arrive.

title: How to use an AED on a child | Paediatric First Aid Refresher | iHASCO
description:
An automated external defibrillator or AED is a life-saving machine. An AED can be used on children over one year old if their heart has stopped beating. It gives the heart an electric shock to start it beating again.

Once an AED has been brought to you, ask someone to help you by switching it on and following the prompts to apply the pads, so that you don’t have to stop giving CPR.

When switched on the AED will immediately start to give you visual and verbal prompts telling you what to do. 

To find out more about first aid procedures and how to perform them on children and babies, follow the link below for your free trial on our Paediatric First Aid Refresher - 
https://www.ihasco.co.uk/courses/detail/paediatric-first-aid-refresher-training
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
VIDEO TRANSCRIPT:

An automated external defibrillator or AED is a life-saving machine. An AED can be used on children over one year old if their heart has stopped beating. It gives the heart an electric shock to start it beating again. 

Once an AED has been brought to you, ask someone to help you by switching it on and following the prompts to apply the pads, so that you don’t have to stop giving CPR.

When switched on the AED will immediately start to give you visual and verbal prompts telling you what to do. The AED prompts will give instructions similar to these:

• Remove all clothing from the child or baby’s chest.
• Make sure the skin is dry.
• Open the bag and take out the pads.
• Pictures on the pads will show you where they should go.
• Remove the backing paper from one pad.
• The first pad should be pressed firmly on to bare skin in the centre of their chest, about level with their nipples and the other pad placed in the centre of their upper back. The pads should be positioned lengthways with the long sides in line with the length of the child’s body.
• Once the pads are in place, the AED will start evaluating their heart’s rhythm.
• It will tell you to stop giving CPR and tell everyone to stand well back.
• It will tell you when it’s preparing to deliver the shock and remind you that everyone must be clear and not touching the child or baby.
• It will then tell you it’s delivering the shock – there’s often an audible beep warning at this point.
• It tells you when the shock has been delivered and tells you to restart chest compressions and rescue breaths. And to continue CPR for 2 minutes before it re-analyses. 

At this point it could say, “No shock advised, continue CPR”. If the child or baby shows signs of becoming responsive, put them in the appropriate recovery position.  Leave the AED attached, so that it can keep monitoring them - in case they stop breathing again.  

Continue to follow the voice and/or visual prompts that the machine gives you until help arrives.

title: How to Give CPR to an Infant
description: Knowing the basics of CPR can help save an infant’s life.
transcript: [CHIMING] CPR is a life-saving action that can get oxygen and blood to the brain in an emergency. Getting trained in CPR is the best way to be prepared, but knowing the basics can help save a life. If a baby doesn't seem to be breathing, shout and tap the bottom of the feet and see if there's any response. Lay the baby face up on a flat, firm surface. Kneel or stand to one side. You may be taught to check for breathing by seeing if the chest is moving, but don't spend more than 10 seconds doing this. Next, shout for help. Have someone call 911 and get an AED, Automated External Defibrillator, if possible, while you start CPR. If you're alone and have a phone, call 911 and then begin CPR. Leave the phone on speaker. If you don't have a phone, do five rounds of CPR, then look for a way to call 911. Start with chest compressions. Place both thumbs side by side in the center of the baby's chest, just below the nipple line, with your other fingers wrapping around, towards the back, like this. You can also do compressions by placing the heel of one hand in the center of the chest, just below the nipple line. Push down fast and hard, about 1.5 inches deep. Let the chest come back up completely after each compression. Do this 30 times. Try to do about two compressions a second. After every 30 compressions, give two rescue breaths. To open the airway, tilt the head back and lift the chin. Put your mouth over the baby's nose and mouth and blow in for about one second. Use just enough air for the chest to rise. After the chest rises and falls, give the second breath. If the chest doesn't rise, reposition the head and chin and try again. Keep doing compressions and rescue breaths until the baby stirs or wakes up or help comes and takes over. Use an AED as soon as one is available. Don't touch patient. Analyzing. Always pause CPR while the AED analyzes for a rhythm and when delivering a shock. Press flashing Shock button. [BEEP] To be better prepared for emergencies, sign up for a life-saving CPR training course from hospitals or other professional organizations. [MUSIC PLAYING] [CHIMING]

Video transcript:
Infant mouth to mouth and nose technique. 

In this video, we will be demonstrating the technique for infant mouth to mouth and nose technique. Follow these steps to give mouth to mouth and nose breaths to an infant. 

Maintain a head tilt/chin lift to keep the airway open. Keep the head in the neutral position. Place your mouth over the infant's mouth and nose to create an airtight seal. Blow into the infant's nose and mouth, pausing to inhale between breaths, to make the chest rise with each breath. If the chest does not rise, repeat the head tilt/chin lift to re-open the airway, and try to give a breath that makes the chest rise. 

When the airway is open, give two breaths that make the chest rise.

description:
Updated for new 2020 AHA / ILCOR guidelines. Choking Baby / Infant First Aid training video by the CPR Certification Institute (Health Ed Solutions Authorized Training Center). Mark Dzwonkiewicz, the lead instructor from Health Ed Solutions, demonstrates the proper way of providing basic life support to a choking conscious infant. He touches on the following updated AHA and ILCOR guidelines:

1️⃣ Perform 5 back blows. Remember to place the heel of the hand right between the scapula. 
2️⃣ If the obstruction doesn't come out, cradle and flip over the infant with the head still down. Perform 5 chest thrusts, 2 fingers just beneath the nipple line and compress about 1/3 the distance between the child's chest.
3️⃣ Look into the airway and check if you can see and remove the object.
4️⃣ If you can't see and remove the object, perform 2 ventilations.

Continue the cycle until the obstruction comes out or until help comes.

title: 7b: Chest Compressions in Infant CPR (2021) OLD
description:
Chest Compressions in Infant CPR is the focus of this lesson. CPR for infants and children is almost identical. The frequency and depth necessary for appropriate compressions is explained. Performing compressions correctly is essential. 

*The newest information for 2022 is available here: https://youtu.be/HWDxG6vpfOk
 
"CPR for infants is almost identical to CPR for children, making steps for compressions just as similar.

In infants, push hard and fast as you would in a child or adult receiving CPR. Position the infant on their back on a firm, hard surface.

Then, move any bulky clothing away from the chest.

Place two fingers of one hand on the breastbone right below the nipple line. 

Push straight down approximately 1.5 inches (that is 4 cm) at a rate of 100 to 120 beats per minute.

Let the chest recoil to its normal positions after every compression. 

Performing compressions correctly is essential and can be physically tiring. If someone else can help, switch off every two minutes while minimizing interruptions during compressions."

description:

What do you do when someone's choking?  You and a friend are out in a restaurant and all of a sudden, they start choking.  I'm going to have my friend Hannah come over here.  We're out, we're having a good time, we're eating and all of the sudden, she seems like she's choking. First, you ask, "Are you OK"?  Oftentimes, the international sign for choking is this. I can't breathe.  Something's going on.  If you're around other people, you want to get them to help you.  If you're in a restaurant or place of business, have someone call out for help and have the people help you out.  Tell them what you're doing.  Don't just attack them because that will just heighten their anxiety and their panic.  What you're going to do is, you're going to stand behind them and you're going to wrap your arms all away around.  You find their belly button with your pinky.  Make a fist.  

Put the pinky on the bellybutton, then roll it up so the knuckle of your thumb is right there and then you thrust.  You pull it in and up, but I'm not going to do it as hard.  In and up.  In and up until they can dislodge whatever is in there and they can breathe again.  Don't go crazy like in the movies and start slapping their back and wrestling.  Sometimes people get carried away and they want to slap your back.  They just end up hurting you.  If the person is pregnant or a larger person and you can't get your arms all away around to where their belly button is, you want to go higher, up to where their breastbone is.  So, say Hannah is pregnant - Congratulations! 

You wrap around.  You find their breastbone.  You do the same thing. In and up.  In and up until they dislodge whatever is in their throat and they can breathe again.  If the person is so big, if you're a small person, and you have a big strapping person with you who's choking and you just can't even do that.  You can assist them in doing a self Heimlich maneuver on a chair or surface that will get to their diaphragm.  You just lean them over.  Talk them through it.  

Stay calm. The more panicky you get, the more panicky they're going to get. They're already in a state of anxiety because they can't breathe, which is normal.  If they lose consciousness and they fall to the floor, you're going to lay them down.  You're going to roll them over and then you're going to do the same thing.  You're going to find the bellybutton, roll up, and you're going to thrust while they're on the floor until that comes out or until help arrives.  Continue trying to do the thrusts and trying to get them to get that out of their throat so they can breathe again.  Stay with them until help arrives.

title: 5a. One-Rescuer BLS for Infants, Basic Life Support (BLS)
description:
Chapter 5 discusses BLS for Infants. Infants are defined as age 0 to 12 months. Determining responsiveness is the first step in BLS for infants. Each step is explained in detail, from assessing the scene to contacting 911 and providing CPR. The differences in treatment for infants are also emphasized. Including, but not limited to, compression depth. Proper AED use and CPR are explained. 

"The first step is to shake their shoulders and shout at the infant to determine if they are responsive. 

Then, asses if they are breathing by putting your ear up to their mouth or by watching their chest. 
If the infant is not responding or breathing, then yell for help. If someone responds, then send them to call 911 and to retrieve an AED. (The AHA emphasizes that cell phones with built-in speaker are available everywhere, so rescuers do not have to leave the scene to call 911.) 

Next, feel for the infant’s brachial pulse for no more than 10 seconds. 

If there is no pulse or you can’t tell, then begin CPR by performing 30 chest compressions followed by two breaths. If you can feel a pulse but the rate is less than 60 beats per minute, begin CPR.

To perform CPR on an infant, have the infant face up on a hard surface. Then, using two fingers, perform compressions in the center of the infant’s chest. Make sure to not press on the end of the sternum as this can cause injury. Also, keep in mind that compression depth for an infant should be about 1.5 inches and at least 100 to 120 compressions per minute.

Perform CPR for about two minutes, which is usually five cycles of 30 compressions and two breaths. If help has not arrived yet, call 911 and retrieve an AED.

Next, use and follow the AED prompts while continuing CPR until EMS arrives or until the infant’s condition normalizes."
