title: How to Give CPR to a Child
description: Knowing the basics of CPR can help save a child’s life.
transcript: CPR is a life-saving action that can get oxygen and blood to the brain in an emergency. Getting trained in CPR is the best way to be prepared, but knowing the basics can help save a life. If a child doesn't seem to be breathing, shout and tap the shoulder and see if there's any response. Lay the child face up on a flat, firm surface. Kneel or stand to one side. You may be taught to check for breathing by seeing if the chest is moving, but don't spend more than 10 seconds doing this. Next, shout for help. Have someone call 911 and get an AED if possible while you start CPR. If you're alone and have a phone, call 911 and then begin CPR. Leave the phone on speaker. If you don't have a phone, do five rounds of CPR, then look for a way to call 911. Start with chest compressions. Put the heel of your hand in the center of the chest. For a small child, you'll use one hand. For a larger child, put your other hand on top with the fingers interlaced. Lock your elbows so that your arms are straight. Your shoulders should be in line with your hands. Push down fast and hard, about 2 inches deep. Let the chest come back up completely after each compression. Do this 30 times. Try to do about two compressions a second. After every 30 compressions, give two rescue breaths. To open the airway, tilt the head back and lift the chin. Pinch the nose closed. Blow into the mouth for about 1 second using just enough air to make the chest rise. After the chest rises and falls, give the second breath. If the chest doesn't rise, reposition the head and chin and try again. Keep doing compressions and rescue breaths until the child stirs or wakes up. Help comes and takes over. Or an AED says a shock is needed. To be better prepared for emergencies, sign up for a life-saving CPR training course from hospitals or other professional organizations.

title: Paediatric BLS - 2021 UK Resuscitation Council key points
description:
The 2021 UK Resuscitation Council guidelines have added a few key points about Paediatric basic life support.

In the paediatric basic life support sequence, rescuers should perform an assessment for signs of life, like circulation, simultaneously with breathing assessment and during the delivery of rescue breaths.  

If there are no signs of life, chest compressions should be started immediately after rescue breaths have been delivered. 

There is an emphasis on rescuers using mobile phones with speaker function to facilitate bystander access to dispatcher guided cardiopulmonary resuscitation known as CPR and to summon emergency medical services (EMS) without leaving the child or infant. 

In certain situations, such as when the child or infant is breathing spontaneously but requires airway management or when the child has a traumatic injury, the recovery position is not recommended. In these circumstances:    

Keep the patient flat, maintain an open airway by either continued head tilt and chin lift or jaw thrust.  

For trauma victims, leave the child or infant lying flat and open and maintain the airway using a jaw thrust, taking care to avoid spinal movement.  

High-quality CPR is emphasised in the guidelines which is obtained by: 

A chest compression depth at least one third the anterior-posterior diameter of the chest, or by 4 cm for the infant and 5 cm for the child. 

The chest compression pauses minimised so that 80% or more of the CPR cycle is comprised of chest compressions chest at a  rate 100-120 per min. And finally by allowing full recoil of the chest after each chest compression.

Transcript:
Si usted llega al lugar

Observe el lugar para determinar las condiciones de seguridad. Verifique si el bebé está consciente. Dele un golpecito suave en el hombro o un golpecito rápido en la parte de abajo del talón y grite.

No hay respuesta

Llame al 911 de inmediato.

Si el bebé está tendido boca abajo, voltéelo y colóquelo boca arriba. El bebé debe estar tendido sobre una superficie plana y firme.

Verifique si está respirando y si hay señales de vida

Observe el pecho para ver si hay movimientos normales. Observe durante no más de 10 segundos para ver si hay señales de vida y si está respirando.

No hay respiración ni señales de vida

Comience la reanimación cardiopulmonar
a.Coloque dos o tres dedos en el centro del esternón del bebé, apenas por debajo de la línea de los pezones.
b.Comprima el pecho 1 ½ pulgadas hacia abajo 30 veces.
c.Después de las compresiones, haga la respiración boca a boca. Incline la cabeza del bebé ligeramente hacia atrás, colocando una mano en la frente y levantando el mentón o barbilla del bebé con dos dedos de la otra mano. Cubra la nariz y la boca del bebé con su boca y haga la respiración soplando dos veces breve y suavemente, prestando atención para observar el pecho del bebé que se levanta.
d.Continúe con 30 compresiones/dos respiraciones, 30 compresiones/dos respiraciones, etc. 

Continúe con la reanimación cardiopulmonar hasta que otro rescatista lo reemplace, hasta que vea señales de vida o hasta que llegue ayuda.

title: CPR in Action | A 3D look inside the body
description:
This 3D animation was designed to share life-saving information with the general public to demonstrate the importance of good, effective CPR! 

Effective compressions create an artificial pump and send oxygenated blood to the brain to keep the brain alive. CPR also keeps blood and oxygen moving through the heart muscle itself so that it has the best chance of being successfully defibrillated when the AED arrives. 

After a Sudden Cardiac Arrest, brain damage will start to set in within 4 minutes and is irreversible after 10 minutes. CPR is the person’s only chance of survival while waiting for an automated external defibrillator to arrive. 

Action First Aid is committed to widespread access, awareness and public education about when and how to use an AED and perform effective CPR. title: Back Blows for Infants | Basic Life Support Training | iHASCO
description:
An infant is a child aged 1 or younger. If their airway becomes blocked, they’re particularly vulnerable as they can’t communicate the fact that they’re choking, so it’s up to you to make sure that you’re able to spot the warning signs.

If the blockage is stopping them from breathing completely, then their skin will begin to look blue or grey, they will get progressively weaker, and will eventually lose consciousness.

Our Basic Life Support Training educates you on what to do if an infant is choking through back blows and chest thrusts. Also covered in this course - what to do if adults or children are choking and basic life support for adults. 

Find out more - https://www.ihasco.co.uk/courses/detail/basic-life-support-in-care-training

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
COUSE TRANSCRIPT 

If the infant can’t cough effectively and is struggling to breathe, you need to start giving back blows.

Remember, don’t try and remove the blockage with your fingers unless it’s clear, obvious, and easy to reach.
 
To give effective back blows to an infant, support them face-down along your thigh, with their head hanging over your knee. Their head should be lower than their bottom allowing gravity to help remove the blockage.

Place one of your hands under their chin, with your thumb and fingers along the angle of their jaw. This’ll help support their head. But don’t squeeze the soft area underneath their jaw otherwise you’ll just make the problem worse.

Use the heel of your other hand to give 5 sharp blows to their back, directly between their shoulder blades.

In this Video: First Aid Instructional Clips - This video illustrates the proper first aid treatment for an infant who is choking.

Check the scene: Ensure that the area is safe for you to approach and check the infant for any signs of responsiveness. Tap the infant's foot and shout, "Are you okay?" If there's no response, proceed to the next steps.

Call for help: If you're alone, perform two minutes of CPR before calling for help. If someone is around, ask them to call for emergency services immediately.

Open the airway: Tilt the head back gently and lift the chin with one hand, while supporting the infant's head with the other hand. Check for breathing.

Perform compressions: Place two fingers on the infant's breastbone and push down about 1 1/2 inches at a rate of 100-120 compressions per minute.

Give rescue breaths: Pinch the infant's nose and breathe into their mouth for one second. Watch for the chest to rise and fall with each breath.

Repeat the compressions and breaths: Continue performing compressions and breaths at a ratio of 30 compressions to 2 breaths. Switch with someone else every two minutes to prevent fatigue.
Keep performing CPR until help arrives or the infant starts to show signs of life.

It's important to note that performing CPR on an infant can be more challenging than on an adult, so it's crucial to take an infant CPR course to learn the technique properly. Additionally, always call for help in an emergency.

title: Infant One-Person BLS (2026)
description:
If the scene is safe, approach the victim and assess their responsiveness. Send another person to activate the emergency response system and get an AED if possible. Assess breathing and check the infant’s pulse. If the infant is not breathing, or only gasping, and you can’t find a pulse, begin CPR starting with compressions. Perform 30 compressions at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute at a depth of at least ⅓ the chest. For infants, this is about 1.5 inches. When the AED is brought to the scene, begin by turning the device on. Remove any clothing from the victim and apply the AED pads, one on the front of the infant’s chest and one on their back. Plug in the connector and then clear the victim while the AED analyzes the rhythm. If no shock is advised, resume CPR beginning with chest compressions. If a shock is advised, clear the victim again before delivering the shock. Once the AED has charged, hit the shock button. After delivering the shock, resume CPR beginning with 30 chest compressions. Open the airway and deliver two breaths, each lasting one second. Watch for chest rise. Begin again with 30 chest compressions and continue at this ratio of 30 compressions to 2 breaths until the AED prompts you to stop or further help arrives.

Video transcript:
In this video we will be showing you the techniques and sequence of child CPR. 

Always make sure the scene is safe for you and the victim. Check for response by tapping the victims shoulder and shout "Are you OK?". If two rescuers are present then activate emergency response system and get or call for AED. If only one rescuer is present and there is no response, that is, if the victim isn't breathing or only gasping shout for help and start CPR. 

Check for carotid pulse for at least 5 seconds but no more than 10 seconds. If you do not feel the pulse or the pulse is less than 60 beats per minute and signs of poor perfusion then begin CPR immediately. Starting with chest compressions. Remember, start compressions within 10 seconds of recognition of cardiac arrest. 

Push hard and fast, at a rate of at least 100 compressions a minute. Count out loud "1, 2, 3,..." up to 30 compressions. After 30 compressions open the airway using the head tilt chin lift method. Give two breaths, deliver air over one second to make the victim's chest rise. Give one breath every 3-5 seconds at a rate of 12-20 breaths per minute. 

Try to limit interruptions in chest compressions to less than 10 seconds. Continue with 30 compressions followed by two ventilations for a ratio of 30:2. Until an advanced airway endotracheal tube, combitube, or laryngeal mask airway is placed. Once the advanced airway is placed then start continuous chest compressions with ventilations at a rate of one breath every 6-8 seconds for a rate of 8-10 ventilations per minute. 

AED with pediatric pads should be used as soon as it is available. Resume chest compressions immediately after the shock is given. Leave to activate emergency response system and get AED or defibrillator only if it has not been activated.

Remember for child CPR with one rescuer only chest compression to ventilation ratio is 30:2. Activate emergency response system and go for AED after 5 cycles or 2 minutes. For child CPR with two rescuers compression to ventilation ratio is 15:2. For two rescuers change the compressor every 5 cycles or 2 minutes to avoid fatigue.

transcript: As a new parent, learning CPR is very important. Thousands of babies are saved every year because someone knew CPR and started it right away. Knowing CPR can help prevent brain damage in your child if they stop breathing. CPR stands for cardiopulmonary resuscitation. CPR helps keep blood and oxygen flowing to the heart and brain when the heart stops. In this video you will learn the basics of infant CPR. Infant CPR is only for babies less than a year old. CPR for children and adults is slightly different. Anyone who cares for an infant should, and can, learn CPR. (Speaker #1) If you find your baby unresponsive or not breathing… 1. Tap the baby’s foot and shout to see if they respond. Never shake a baby. 2. If the baby does not respond, yell for help. 3. If someone comes, tell them to call 911. 4. Check for breathing. 5. If the baby is not breathing, they need CPR right away. 6. Carefully move the baby to a firm, flat surface, above ground. 7. Place two fingers in the middle of the baby’s chest, just below the nipple line. 8. Give 30 compressions by pressing straight down about 1 ½ inches. 9. Push hard and fast, at least 100 compressions per minute, and let the chest rise all the way back up after each push. 10. Next, give two breaths by putting your mouth over the baby’s mouth and nose. 11. Gently give enough breath to make the baby’s chest rise. 12. Keep alternating two breaths and 30 compressions until the baby responds or trained help arrives. If the baby is still unresponsive after two minutes of CPR and you have no help to call 911, carry the baby with you to the phone, and make the call yourself. You can continue giving compressions and breaths with the baby in a football hold. Every five days in the United States, at least one child dies from choking. When an infant is choking, quick action can be lifesaving. Continue watching to learn what to do when a child is choking. If a baby is choking but is able to cough and breathe, allow them to do so. It allows their own reflexes to clear the airway. If you know a baby is choking and they are having trouble breathing or they stop breathing, begin a sequence of five back slaps and five chest thrusts. This is what it looks like: 1. Hold the baby face down on your forearm with its head lower than its body. Make sure the baby’s head and neck are supported. 2. Give five firm slaps on the baby’s back with the heel of your hand. Deliver the slap between the baby’s shoulder blades. 3. If the object does not come out, turn the baby over onto their back. 4. Support the head and neck with your arm, and keep the baby’s head below their body. 5. Now give five chest thrusts. Use two fingers and press down in the middle of the baby’s chest just below the nipple line, like you did in CPR. 6. Repeat five back blows and five chest thrusts until a. The object is coughed up b. The baby begins to breathe, or c. The baby becomes unconscious 7. If the baby becomes unconscious, follow the steps of infant CPR that you’ve already learned 8. Each time you give breaths, look to see if the object has come out. 9. If you see an object in the mouth, take it out. Any baby that receives CPR or choking treatment should be seen by a doctor to make sure they’re all right. Thank you for watching this video. Please practice with a nurse and on a mannequin until you feel comfortable doing it on your own.

title: 6e: AED for Children (2026)
description:
The fifth lesson in chapter six discusses AED use in children. There are step-by-step directions for use provided. It is important to follow the prompts on the AED. 

An AED can deliver a pediatric shock to restart the heart. The steps for using an AED in children are the same as those in adults. Always check the AED when it arrives on the scene. If the child is younger than eight years, then use pediatric pads. If pediatric pads are not available, standard, that is adult pads, may be used. If you are using standard pads, make sure that the pads do not overlap each other. If needed, put one of the pads on the child’s back.

Some AEDs have a switch that can be set to deliver a pediatric shock. If available, turn this switch on when using AED for children younger than eight years. If the AED cannot deliver a pediatric shock, an adult shock should be given. Be sure to start CPR.

To use an AED on a child, first, turn the power on.
Expose the child’s chest. Then, apply the pads. Ensure that the pads do not touch.
Connect the pads.
Clear the child so no one is touching the child. Analyze the rhythm.
Follow the prompts: Shock Advised, No Shock Advised, Check Connection, etc. Resume CPR with compressions.

title: Learn Infant CPR - How to Do Infant CPR
description:
Would you know what to do if you found an unresponsive infant? This video will show you how to perform infant CPR.

Go here http://www.onlinecprcertification.net/ to learn how to correctly perform safety skills like this for FREE. CPR training and first aid training materials are developed by board certified physicians.

Follow us on Twitter: https://twitter.com/AACPRFirstAid -- @AACPRFirstAid

Like us on Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/pages/OnlineCPRCertificationnet/196003870528190

Video transcript: 
In this video, we will be showing you the techniques and sequence of an infant CPR. Always make sure the scene is safe for you and the victim. Check for response by tapping the infant's feet or the shoulder. 
If two rescuers are present, then activate emergency response system and get or call for AED. If only one rescuer is present, and there is no response, that is if the infant is unresponsive and not breathing or only gasping, then shout for help and start CPR.

Immediately start the chest compressions. Position two fingers in the center of the chest, below the nipple line. Press the infant's breastbone down at least 1/3 the depth of the chest, approximately 1 1/2 inches or 4 centimeters. Compress at the rate of at least 100 per minute, and count out loud, "1, 2, 3, 4, 5" up to 30 compressions. After each compression, allow the chest to recoil completely. 

After 30 compressions, perform a head tilt/chin lift to open the airway. Keep the head in neutral position--if you extend an infant's head beyond the neutral position, the infant's airway may become blocked. Give two breaths. Deliver air over one second to make the infant's chest rise. Give one breath every 3-5 second interval, or 12-20 breaths per minute. Try to limit interruptions in chest compressions to less than 10 seconds. 

Continue 30 compressions to 2 ventilations; that is a ratio of 30:2. After 5 cycles, or two minutes, leave to activate to emergency medical services and to get AED only if emergency response system has not been activated. 

Use an AED with pediatric pads as soon as it is available. Resume chest compressions immediately after the shock is given. 

Remember, for infant CPR with only one rescuer, chest compressions to ventilation ratio is 30:2. Activate emergency response cystem after five cycles, or two minutes. For infant CPR with two rescuers, compression to ventilation ratio is 15:2. For two rescuers, change the compressor rescuer every five cycles, or two minutes, to avoid fatigue. Rescuers should try to change compressor role in less than five seconds.

title: How to do CPR on a Child who has a Trach Tube (Ages 1 to 12 Years)
description:
http://www.cincinnatichildrens.org/cpr
Cincinnati Children's Demonstrates Child CPR with Tracheostomy (Ages 1 to 12 Years).

Transcript:
You arrive on the scene: Check the scene for safety

Check the child for consciousness. Gently tap the shoulder and shout. 

No Response

Call 911 immediately.  

If the child is lying on his stomach, turn him over onto his back. The child should be lying on a hard flat surface.

Check for Breathing and Signs of Life

Watch their chest for any normal movement.  Look for signs of life and breathing for no more than 10 seconds. 

No Breathing or Signs of Life

Begin CPR:

1. Position the heel of one hand on the center of the child's chest; place your other hand on top.

2. With your elbows locked and straight, lean over the child’s chest and compress the chest 2 inches in depth 30 times. 

3. After the compressions, give breaths using a resuscitation bag attached to the trach.  Gently squeeze the bag and give 2 breaths – just enough to make the chest rise.

4. Continue with 30 compressions / 2 breaths, 30 compressions / 2 breaths, etc. 

If Breaths Do Not Make Chest Rise

a. Suction the trach tube. If the trach has an inner cannula, remove it and suction the length of the trach tube.

b. Change the trach if it is plugged or dislodged.

c. Give 2 breaths to the trach using a resuscitation bag.

Continue CPR until you see signs of life, another rescuer takes over, or help arrives.

For more information visit: http://www.cincinnatichildrens.org/cpr

title: Moment six-year-old saves little sister from choking with Heimlich maneuver | SWNS
description:
This is the moment a young girl saved her little sister from choking on a sweet - using the Heimlich maneuver.

Doudou, six, and her younger sister Woniu, three, were spending an evening at home in Hainan Province, China, when Woniu started choking.

Video captured in August shows Woniu rushing into the living room to find Doudou and show her that she had something stuck in her throat.

Doudou immediately jumped into action, stood up and started performing the Heimlich maneuver on her littler sister.

Doudou had seen her mother perform the Heimlich before on Woniu, which is how she knew how to act so quickly.

After several attempts, Woniu eventually spits out the sweet.

Disclaimer - This video is for training purposes only. If it is an emergency please call Triple Zero (000). 

To find out more about enrolling in a Resuscitation course with Royal Life Saving visit:   https://www.royallifesaving.com.au/training/resuscitation

A family member is the first on the scene in most emergency situations. In fact many children are alive today because their parents knew how to perform CPR and responded quickly. For this reason alone, Royal Life Saving encourages everyone to learn CPR.

Having the skills to respond in an emergency situation can mean the difference between life and death.

Resuscitation or Cardio Pulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) involves stimulating the heart and breathing air into the lungs to preserve or restore life. Resuscitation involves establishing or maintaining an airway, breathing and circulation.

Royal Life Saving has a number of CPR related resources and courses available including a CPR chart that can be used near your backyard swimming pool and CPR courses that are run in a variety of locations across all States and Territories.

title: CPR Lifeline AHA Infant BLS Rescue Breathing with VAM
description:
Respiratory support can be lifesaving for infants when they are not breathing adequately. In this tutorial, we demonstrate infant breathing using a bag-valve mask (BVM) under AHA BLS guidelines, leveraging the RQI HeartCode Complete platform and a Voice-Activated Manikin (VAM). You’ll see how to apply the correct technique, maintain a good mask seal, and respond to feedback in real time.
This video is ideal for healthcare providers, pediatric staff, neonatal teams, instructors, and anyone tasked with maintaining high-quality infant resuscitation skills. By combining visual demonstration with dynamic feedback, learners can internalize effective technique and confidence.
________________________________________
🔍 What You’ll See
• Setup of the RQI + VAM system for infant mode
• Proper head positioning (neutral / slight sniffing position) or technique for infants
• Mask placement over both nose and mouth with secure sealing
• Gentle ventilation and observing for visible chest rise
• Recognizing and managing leaks or imperfect technique as prompted by VAM
• Adjustments in airflow, mask seal, or positioning mid-practice
• How VAM prompts corrections to help you refine your technique
• Best practices & troubleshooting common errors
________________________________________
✅ Why This Matters for Your Training & Clients
• Feedback loop: The VAM’s real-time voice cues help learners self-correct, improving retention
• Visual + tactile learning: Videos strengthen muscle memory before in-person practice
• Demonstrates your training sophistication: Show prospective clients you use advanced simulation tools
• Higher standard training: Helps learners maintain skill proficiency between formal courses
• Confidence building: Seeing correct technique in action reduces hesitation during real events
________________________________________
📝 Clinical Notes & Guidelines
• Infant rescue breathing / ventilation: when an infant has a pulse but inadequate or absent breathing, deliver gentle breaths at around 1 breath every 2–3 seconds (i.e. ~20–30 breaths/min)
• Ventilation volume must be modest—just enough to see chest rise
• A proper mask seal over both nose and mouth is critical (infants breathe through both)
• Watch for excessive pressure or volume that could lead to gastric inflation
• If chest rise is inadequate, reposition airway, re-seal mask, or reassess technique
• Real-time feedback significantly enhances error correction and performance consistency

title: Infant Choking CPR - What to Do If a Baby Is Choking
description:
Would you know what to do if your baby was choking?

Go here http://www.onlinecprcertification.net/ to learn how to correctly perform safety skills like this for FREE. CPR training and first aid training materials are developed by board certified physicians.

Follow us on Twitter: https://twitter.com/AACPRFirstAid -- @AACPRFirstAid

Like us on Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/pages/OnlineCPRCertificationnet/196003870528190

Video transcript: 
In this video, you will learn how to relieve choking in a responsive infant. A choking infant cannot cough or cry, and may quickly start turning blue.

You need to expel the foreign object. Kneel or sit with the infant in your lap. Hold the infant face down. Support the infant's head and jaw with your hand. Rest your forearm on your lap or your thigh to support the infant. Deliver 5 back blows forcefully between the infant's shoulderblades using the heel of your hand. Deliver each blow with sufficient force to attempt to dislodge the foreign body.

After delivering 5 back blows, place your free hand on the infant's back, supporting the back of the infant's head with the palm of your hand. With the palm of the other hand, support the infant's head and turn the infant as a unit.

Hold the infant face up. Keep the infant's head lower than the rest of the body. Provide five quick downward chest thrusts in the middle of the chest over the lower half of the breastbone. Deliver chest thrusts at a rate of about one per second, each with the intention of creating enough force to dislodge the foreign body. 

Repeat the sequence of 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts until the object is removed or the infant becomes unresponsive.

"An AED can deliver a pediatric shock to restart the heart. The steps for using an AED in children are the same as those in adults. Always check the AED when it arrives on the scene. If the child is younger than eight years, then use pediatric pads. If pediatric pads are not available, standard, that is adult pads, may be used. If you are using standard pads, make sure that the pads do not overlap each other. If needed, put one of the pads on the child’s back.

Some AEDs have a switch that can be set to deliver a pediatric shock. If available, turn this switch on when using AED for children younger than eight years. If the AED cannot deliver a pediatric shock, an adult shock should be given. 

To use an AED on a child, first turn the power on.

Expose the child’s chest. Then, apply the pads. Ensure that the pads do not touch.

Connect the pads to the AED.

Clear the child and analyze the rhythm.

Follow the prompts on the AED. If the AED prompts for shock delivery, then clear the child again and press the shock button once the AED has charged. After shock delivery, resume CPR starting with chest compressions. If there is no shock to be delivered, then resume CPR starting with chest compressions."

title: How To Survive Choking With Back Blows
description:
A foreign body airway obstruction (choking) is a life-threatening emergency following the lodgement 
of a foreign object in the casualty’s airway. In some instances, the object lodges at the epiglottis, the entry to the airway, but does not actually enter the airway itself. Both situations cause initial coughing, which is the body’s reflex action to dislodge the object.

Conscious Casualty (Adult and children over 1yr of age)

Position yourself to give back blows
1. Stand or sit with infant face down over your forearm supporting the infants head by holding the cheekbones between thumb and middle finger. Ensure infant’s jaw is relaxed so object can escape the mouth. Place your arm, with infant, over your thigh, head down at approx. 45 degrees, then give a firm, sharp blow between the shoulder blades using the heal of your hand. Ensure your fingers are raised, so as not to accidentally hit the back of the infant’s head.
2. Repeat this up to 5 times, pausing between each blow to check if airway is cleared.
3. If back blows are unsuccessful, deliver up to 5 chest thrusts. The infant should be placed on their back across the rescuer’s thigh
4. Check airway after each chest thrust
5. Repeat cycles of back blows and chest thrusts if obstruction not relieved

title: How to Help a Choking Child or Adult (Everyone Must Know!)
description:
How to Help a Choking Victim. You never know what might happen and when you might need to know how to save someone who's choking. It's important that you learn how to find out if someone's is really choking next to you and how to help people in trouble. You'll have to know how to perform the Heimlich maneuver and there are special rules for how to save a choking child or choking dog. 

Music: https://www.youtube.com/audiolibrary/music

TIMESTAMPS
Assess the situation 0:33
Encourage them to cough 1:13
If the person can’t cough, slap their back 1:55
If the person can’t breathe, perform the Heimlich maneuver 2:46
Helping an unconscious person 3:39
Helping yourself 4:22
Helping pregnant women and obese people 5:24
Saving a choking infant 5:58
Saving a choking child 6:38
Saving an unconscious child 7:11
Saving a choking dog 8:03

SUMMARY
-Determine if the airway obstruction is partial or total to figure out what you should do to help.
-Coughing is the most effective way to clear the airways and push the stuck piece of food out of the trachea.
-Deliver up to 5 strong blows between the shoulder blades using the heel of your hand.
-Perform the Heimlich maneuver to drive out the stuck object.
-If the victim has passed out, lay them down on their back, and vigorously push the abdomen towards the diaphragm until the airway is clear again.
-Start coughing, and if it doesn’t help, perform the Heimlich maneuver on yourself.
-Place your hands as close to the abdomen as possible, higher than you normally would and perform the Heimlich maneuver.
-If the victim is less than a year old, lay them face down on your forearm, make five quick blows right between the infant’s shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
-Stand behind the child or if they’re really small, get on your knees. Clench one hand into a fist and place it between the ribs and belly button with your thumb inwards, move your elbows to the sides and press the child’s stomach.
-If the infant or child is unconscious, try laying them on their back first and try to remove the stuck objects with your fingers. If the child still isn’t breathing or if you were unable to dislodge the object from the start, begin chest compressions.
-Open the dog’s mouth with one hand on the upper jaw and the other on the lower, carefully remove the stuck object with a set of pliers. If and only if nothing else helps, administer the Heimlich maneuver.

In this video we will show you the technique for adult and child chest compression. 
Position yourself on the victim's side, place the heel of one hand on the center of the chest on the lower half of the breast bone. Place the heel of the other hand on top of the first hand. With arms straight, elbows locked and shoulders directly over your hands about 90 degrees to the chest start compressions. Count out loud, "1, 2, 3, 4, 5" up to 20 compressions. Push hard and fast at a rate of at least 100 compression per minute. Push the chest at least 2 inches or 5 centimeters deep with each compression. After each compression allow the chest to return to the original position.

title: How to Help Someone Who Is Choking - Heimlich Maneuver
description:
Do you know how to help someone when they are choking? Watch this video and visit  http://www.onlinecprcertification.net/  to learn more. 

Follow us on Twitter: https://twitter.com/AACPRFirstAid -- @AACPRFirstAid

Like us on Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/pages/OnlineCPRCertificationnet/196003870528190

Video transcript:
In this video you will learn how to relieve choking on an adult and on a child. Use abdominal thrust to relieve chocking in a responsive victim one year of age or older.

Do not use abdominal thrust to relieve choking in infants. If you see someone clutching their throat with their thumb and fingers this is the universal sign for choking. You should ask them are you choking? If they cannot respond or simply nod yes, stand or kneel behind the victim and wrap your arms around the victims waist. Make a fist with one hand, place the thumb side of your fist against the victims abdomen in the mid-line slightly above the navel and well below the breast bone. Grasp your fist with your other hand and press your fist into the victims abdomen with a quick forceful upward thrust. 

Repeat thrusts until the object is expelled from the air way or the victim becomes unresponsive. Give each new thrust with a separate, distinct movement to relieve the obstruction.

https://www.ProFirstAid.com Once a child choking victim becomes unconscious, activate EMS. Check for breathing and the object in the patient's mouth, sweep out if possible. title: Magill forceps for airway foreign body removal
description:
Airway foreign bodies should be removed by a specialist in a controlled environment whenever possible. As an emergency care provider, If you’re ever in a situation where a foreign body is completely obstructing the airway and the patient is decompensating, this may be impossible. After BLS maneuvers (back blows/chest thrusts/abdominal thrusts depending on age), you need to be prepared to remove the foreign body yourself. This means knowing how to properly use Magill forceps. Hold them in your right hand, with your thumb and index fingers in the loops as shown. The forceps are contoured to follow the shape of the oropharynx while keeping your hand out of your field of vision. Insert the laryngoscope, and if you visualize the foreign body, grasp it with the Magill forceps. Then remove both the laryngoscope and Magill forceps at the same time. If you don’t remove the laryngoscope with the Magill forceps, you may unintentionally knock the foreign body loose as you move it past the laryngoscope.

The Magill forceps were designed by Ivan Magill 100 years ago to facilitate nasal intubation. They were designed to keep the field of vision clear, and the blunt rounded tips help avoid injury to tissues and equipment. Incredible that we are still using them!

If they don't respond, I'm going to activate the speaker function on my mobile phone and call the emergency medical services or I'm going to ask a bystander to go and call the emergency medical services for me and ask them to get me a defibrillator. I'm then going to open the casualty's airway. I do this by placing one hand on their forehead, two fingers under the chin, and I tip the head back, but only so slightly. It's a neutral airway we're looking for. It is not a overextension of the neck. I'm then going to look, listen, and feel for normal breathing for up to 10 seconds. And if they're not breathing normally, I'm going to give five initial rescue breaths. Now, when I give my initial rescue breaths, I'm going to put my mouth over the infant's mouth and nose. And I'm going to blow in using a cheek full of air, being careful not to overinflate the infant's lungs. When I blow, I am also going to then look, make sure it's gone in, and also to breathe in fresh air. After I've given five initial rescue breaths, I'm then going to perform 15 chest compressions and two rescue breaths. Now, when I perform a chest compression, I'm going to push down 1/3 of their body depth. And I'm going to use two thumbs to do this because infant is quite small. I'm going to place one thumb on top of of the other one. And I'm going to aim on the lower breast bone and the center of the chest and push down 15 times at the speed of 100 120 beats per minute. After 15 chest compressions, I'm then going to do two rescue breaths and I'm going to just keep on going. Now, if nobody has called emergency medical services, I will keep performing CPR for one minute before I take baby with me to go and make that phone call. and then I would carry on. I will talk about the use of the AED in later videos.

title: OLD 1a: Initiating the Chain of Survival (Adult and Pediatrics)
description:
An introduction to the General Concepts of Basic Life Support. This video discusses the BLS Adult and Pediatric Chains of Survival. Knowing which actions to take and being efficient in their execution can make the difference in a life-or-death cardiac arrest situation. There are appropriate actions for both the Adult Chain of Survival and Pediatric Chain of Survival. Both of which are reviewed in this lesson. 

"Taking the right action quickly and confidently can make the difference between life and death for an individual dealing with cardiac arrest. When you find someone who is in need of help, quickly start and follow the steps from the appropriate Chain of Survival.

The first step in the Adult Chain of Survival is to recognize symptoms and activate EMS by calling 911. Next, perform early CPR by providing high-quality chest compressions to circulate oxygen. Upon the arrival of the AED, turn it on and follow the prompts (defibrillate if advised). Once the EMS team arrives, they will provide advanced life support to the individual. When the individual becomes stable and is taken to the hospital, they will receive post-cardiac arrest care.

Now let’s review the Pediatric Chain of Survival.

Emergencies in children and infants are not usually caused by the heart. Children and infants most often have breathing problems that trigger cardiac arrest. The first and most important step of the Pediatric Chain of Survival is prevention. This means if you come across a child or infant who is experiencing breathing problems, take immediate action. In the case that the heart does stop, perform high-quality CPR. If they are still unresponsive after performing CPR, then activate EMS by calling 911. Then, the EMS team will perform advanced life support. After they are stable and taken to the hospital, they will receive post-cardiac arrest care."

title: 7b. Chest Compressions in infant CPR (Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation) (2018) OLD
description:
Chest Compressions in Infant CPR is the focus of this lesson. CPR for infants and children is almost identical. The frequency and depth necessary for appropriate compressions is explained. Performing compressions correctly is essential. 
 
"CPR for infants is almost identical to CPR for children, making steps for compressions just as similar.

In infants, push hard and fast as you would in a child or adult receiving CPR. Position the infant on a firm, hard surface to make giving CPR easier.

Then, move any clothing away from the chest.

Place two fingers of one hand on the breastbone right below the nipple line. 

Push straight down approximately 1.5 inches (that is 4 cm) at a rate of 100 to 120 beats per minute.

Let the chest recoil to its normal positions after every compression. 

Performing compressions correctly is essential and can be physically tiring. If someone else can help, switch off every two minutes while minimizing interruptions during compressions."

In this video, we will be demonstrating the technique for infant CPR with two rescuers. 

Utilize the two-thumb, encircling-hands chest compression technique. Place both hands side by side in the center of the infant's chest on the lower half of the breastbone. Encircle the infant's chest and support the infant's back with the fingers of both hands. With your hands encircling the chest, use both  thumbs to depress the breastbone approximately one-third the depth of the infant's chest, 1 1/2 inches, or 4 centimeters. 

Deliver compressions in a smooth fashion at a rate of at least 100 compressions per minute. After each compression, allow the chest to recoil completely. After 15 compressions, pause briefly for the second rescuer to open the airway with a head titl/chin lift and give two breaths. The chest should rise with each breath. 

Remember, for infant CPR with two rescuers, the compression to ventilation ratio is 15:2. For two rescuers, change the compressor every five cycles or 2 minutes to avoid fatigue. Rescuers should try to change the compressor role in less than 5 seconds.

title: 3b. One-Rescuer BLS in Children, Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS)
description:
This is a lesson about the administration of basic life support specifically in situations involving children. It provides a step-by-step overview of what to do in one-rescuer scenario involving children. There are important adjustments which must be made when administering CPR to a child, which are highlighted here, along with important information about maintaining the situation until EMS arrives on the scene.

"If you are alone with a child in a life-threatening situation, first shake their shoulders and talk loudly to them to determine if they are responsive.

Then, assess their breathing.

If the child does not respond and is not breathing (or is only gasping for air), then yell for help. If someone responds, send them to call 911 and get an AED (if you are not in a health care facility), or activate emergency response system and get a defibrillator (if you are in a health care facility). 

Feel for the child’s carotid pulse on the side of their neck or femoral pulse on the inner thigh in the crease between their leg and groin. Feel for no more than 10 seconds.

If you cannot feel a pulse, or if you are unsure that you feel a pulse, begin CPR by doing 30 compressions followed by two breaths. If you can feel a pulse but the pulse rate is less than 60 beats per minute, begin CPR. This rate is too slow for a child.

After doing CPR for about two minutes, which is usually five cycles of 30 compressions and two breaths, and if help has not arrived, call EMS while staying with the child. The AHA emphasizes to use speaker-equipped cell phones that are available everywhere now. 

Get an AED or a defibrillator if you know where one is. Use and follow the prompts on the AED or the defibrillator while continuing CPR until EMS arrives or until child’s condition normalizes."

title: How to do CPR on an Infant (Ages Newborn to 1 Year)
description:
http://www.cincinnatichildrens.org/cpr-infant
Cincinnati Children's Demonstrates Adult CPR (Ages 12 and Older).

Transcript:
You Arrive on the Scene

Check the scene for safety. Check the infant for consciousness. Gently tap the shoulder or flick the bottom of the heel and shout.

No Response

Call 911 immediately.  

If the infant is on his or her stomach, turn the infant over onto his or her back.  The infant should be lying on a hard flat surface.

Check for Breathing and Signs of Life

Watch the chest for any normal movement.  Look for signs of life and breathing for no more than 10 seconds. 

No Breathing or Signs of Life

Begin CPR

a. Position two or three fingers on the center of the infant’s breastbone, just below the nipple line.

b. Compress the chest 1½ inches in depth 30 times.

c. After giving compressions, give breaths. Tilt the infant's head back, slightly, using  one hand on the forehead and lifting up on the infant's chin with two fingers of your other hand. Cover both the infant’s nose and mouth with your mouth and give two small, slow breaths, watching for the infant’s chest to rise.

d. Continue with 30 compressions / two breathes, 30 compressions / two breathes, etc. 

Continue CPR until another rescuer takes over, you see signs of life or help arrives.

For more information visit: http://www.cincinnatichildrens.org/cpr-infant

title: CPR Training Video - How to Perform Adult and Child Rescue Breathing
description:
Knowing how to perform rescue breathing can save someone's life.

Go here http://www.onlinecprcertification.net/ to learn how to correctly perform safety skills like this for FREE. CPR training and first aid training materials are developed by board certified physicians.

Follow us on Twitter: https://twitter.com/AACPRFirstAid -- @AACPRFirstAid

Like us on Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/pages/OnlineCPRCertificationnet/196003870528190

Video transcript: 
In this video, you will learn the techniques and sequence of how to perform adult and child rescue breathing. 

Always make sure the scene is safe for you and the victim. Check for response by tapping the victim's shoulder and shouting, "Are you okay?"

If there is no response, that is, if the victim is unresponsive and not breathing or only gasping, then activate emergency response system and get or call for an AED. Check for the carotid pulse. Check the pulse for at least 5 seconds, but no more than 10 seconds. If the pulse is present, the start rescue breathing.

Open the airway using head tilt/chin lift. Give two breaths. Deliver each breath in one second duration, looking for the chest to rise. If the first breath does not make the chest rise and fall, then reposition the head, i.e. head tilt/chin lift, and readminister the breaths. 

Continue rescue breathing every 5-6 seconds, that is about 10-12 breaths per minute. Deliver each breath over one second. Check the carotid pulse every two minutes.

title: Infant Choking | Singapore Emergency Responder Academy, First Aid and CPR Training
description:
In some cases, infants might choke on foreign objects like food or small toys. It is important for the emergency responder to know what to do to clear the infant's airway.

1) Recognise signs by accessing airway. Some signs include loss of voice, increase breathing difficulty, and the infant's face turns blue.
2) Support the infant by using the sandwich maneuver
3) Support the head of the infant with your palm, and back of the infant's body on your forearm
4) Sandwich the infant with your other hand by supporting the infant's jaw with your thumb on one side, and the rest of your fingers on the other side
5) Place your forearm on the infant's chest
6) Straddle the infant faced down, with the head lower than the body
7) Use your knee as a support
8) Use the heel of your free hand to deliver 5 back blows between the infant's shoulder blades
9) Turn the infant from the back blow position 
10) Draw an imaginary line between the nipples with your ring finger
11) At the sternum, place your middle and index fingers next to your ring finger
12) Lift up your ring finger and deliver 5 chest thrusts over the lower half of the sternum using the same location and technique as chest compressions in CPR
13) If a foreign body is seen, remove the foreign body with your middle finger
14) Repeat the back blow and chest thrust technique until the foreign body is expelled or the infant becomes unconscious

title: Child CPR - How to Administer CPR to a Child
description:
Would you know what to do if you found your child unresponsive and not breathing? Learn child CPR with this video.

Go here http://www.onlinecprcertification.net/ to learn how to correctly perform safety skills like this for FREE. CPR training and first aid training materials are developed by board certified physicians.

Follow us on Twitter: https://twitter.com/AACPRFirstAid -- @AACPRFirstAid

Like us on Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/pages/OnlineCPRCertificationnet/196003870528190

Video transcript: 
Child CPR. In this video, we will be showing you the techniques and sequence of child CPR.

1. Always make sure the scene is safe for you and the victim.
2. Check for response by tapping the victim's shoulder and shout, "Are you okay?"
3. If two rescuers are present, then activate emergency medical services and get or call for an AED. 
4. If only one rescuer is present, and if there is no response, that is, if the victim is unresponsive and not breathing, or only gasping, then shout for help and start CPR. 
5. Immediately start with chest compressions. Push hard and fast, at a rate of 100 beats per minute. Count out loud "1, 2, 3, 4, 5" up to 30 compressions. For very small children, you may use either one or two hands for chest compressions. 
6. Push the chest at least 1/3 the depth of the chest, or approximately 2 inches.
7. After 30 compressions, open the airway and give a breath using the head tilt/chin lift method. Give two breaths. Deliver air over one second to make the victim's chest rise.
8. Give one breath every 3 to 5 seconds for a rate of 12-20 breaths per minute.
9. Try to limit the interruptions in chest compressions to less than 10 seconds. 
10. Continue 30 compressions followed by 2 ventilations, that is a ratio of 30:2.

An AED with pediatric pads which are suitable for children 1-8 years of age should be used as soon as it is available. Resume chest compressions immediately after the shock is given.

Leave to activate emergency medical services to to get an AED or defibrillator only if emergency medical services has not already been activated. 

Remember, for child CPR with only one rescuer, chest compression to ventilation is 30:2. Activate emergency response system and call for AED after 5 cycles, or two minutes. For child CPR with two rescuers, compression/ventilation ratio is 15:2.  For two rescuers, change the compressor every two minutes or every 5 cycles to avoid fatigue. Rescuers should try to change the compressor role in less than 5 seconds.

transcript: If you ever find your baby is not responding to you, you will give them the best chance of survival if you know what to do. If you have found your baby unresponsive and not breathing normally, you'll need to perform baby CPR. Call for help. Ask a helper to call 999 or 112 for emergency help. Use a mobile speakerphone if you're on your own, so you can start CPR as soon as possible. If you're on your own and you don't have a speakerphone, you need to do CPR for a minute before you can call for help. Place them on a firm surface and open their airway. With one hand on the forehead, gently tilt their head back. With your finger tip, gently lift the chin to open the airway. Pick out any visible obstructions from the mouth and nose. Step one is 'puff'. Take a breath, put your lips around your baby's mouth and nose make a seal. Blow gently and steadily for up to one second. The chest should rise. Remove your mouth and watch the chest fall. That's one rescue breath or 'puff'. Do this five times. Step two is 'pump', or chest compressions. Put two fingers in the centre of your baby's chest and push down a third of the depth of the chest. Release the pressure, allowing the chest to come back up before pressing back down again. Repeat this 30 times at a rate of 100-120 pumps per minute. This is quite quick. After 30 chest pumps, open the airway and give a further two puffs. Continue to alternate between thirty chest pumps and two puffs. If you're on your own and don't have a speakerphone, stop after one minute and call 999 or 112 for emergency help. If a mobile phone is not available and you have to move to get to a telephone, take the baby with you. Keep repeating 30 pumps then two puffs until help arrives or they become responsive. So remember: if your baby's unresponsive and not breathing, call for help. Ask a helper to call 999 or 112 for emergency help. If you're on your own use the speakerphone and start CPR soon as possible. If you don't have a speakerphone, do CPR for a minute before calling for emergency help. Give five initial puffs, covering both the nose and mouth, then 30 chest pumps with two fingers to the centre of the chest. Continue CPR with 30 pumps and two puffs until help arrives. And that's how you do baby CPR. Thanks for watching. Help support St John Ambulance. Donate today.

title: Back Blows for Children | Basic Life Support | iHASCO
description:
Between the age of 1 and the onset of puberty, the size, and physical and mental abilities of a child vary wildly. You’ll need to use your judgement as to whether they need your help and exactly what they need you to do. 

If they’re coughing effectively, you don’t need to step in just yet – coughing should usually be enough to remove the blockage. However, you should keep a close eye on them and if their coughing becomes ineffective or they start turning blue, you’ll need to act. 

Our Basic Life Support Training will educate you on how to treat a child who you believe is choking as well as performing CPR on a child (aged between 1 and the onset of puberty).

Find out more - https://www.ihasco.co.uk/courses/detail/basic-life-support-in-care-training
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
COURSE TRANSCRIPT

If the child is conscious but struggling to breathe or has stopped breathing altogether, begin giving them back blows.

They’re more effective if the child is positioned with their head down, so that gravity can do most of the work. Lie them across your lap, if possible, or if they’re too big for that, support them as they lean forward with their head down.

Use the heel of your hand to give 5 sharp blows between their shoulder blades. Then move onto abdominal thrusts.

title: How to do CPR on a Child (Ages 1 to 12 Years)
description:
http://www.cincinnatichildrens.org/cpr-children
Cincinnati Children's Demonstrates Child CPR (Ages 1 to 12 Years).

Transcript:
You Arrive on the Scene

Check the scene for safety.  Check the child for consciousness. Gently tap the shoulder and shout.

No Response

Call 911 immediately.  

If the child is on his or her stomach, turn the child over onto his or her back. The child should be lying on a hard flat surface.

Check for Breathing and Signs of Life

Watch the chest for any normal movement.  Look for signs of life and breathing for no more than 10 seconds. 

No Breathing or Signs of Life

Begin CPR

a. Position one hand on the center of the child's chest; place your other hand on top.

b. With your elbows locked and arms straight, lean over the child’s chest and compress the child's chest 2 inches in depth 30 times.

c. After the compressions, give breaths. Give breaths by tilting the head back, lifting the chin, and pinch the nose. Place your mouth over the child’s mouth and give two slow, gentle breaths – just enough to make the chest rise.

d. Continue with 30 compressions / two breathes, 30 compressions / two breathes, etc. 

Continue CPR until another rescuer takes over, you see signs of life or help arrives.

title: What To Do If Someone Is Choking | In Case of Emergency | Mass General Brigham
description:
For more information on choking first aid: https://www.massgeneralbrigham.org/en/about/newsroom/articles/choking-first-aid 

What should you do if someone is choking? Melisa W. Lai-Becker, MD, Emergency Medicine Physician at Mass General Brigham, discusses how to respond to someone choking, and how to perform the Heimlich maneuver on adults and infants. Choking symptoms include a person not being able to make a sound, holding their neck, or turning color in their face. Call for emergency help immediately and begin providing care. First, try hitting between the shoulder blades, firmly and sharply with the heel of your hand, 5 times. If that doesn’t work, begin doing the Heimlich maneuver, where you stand behind the choking person and give firm abdominal thrusts above their belly button. For infants, hold them face down with their bottoms above their heads, and hit firmly on the back 5 times. Keep alternating back blows and the Heimlich maneuver until medical help arrives. Choking can happen anywhere and anytime, but by staying calm and providing care, you can help save a life.

title: How to perform Child CPR with an AED
description:
If you see an infant or child collapse, CPR can save their life. Rescue breaths are especially important when performing CPR on a child in cardiac arrest. To give CPR to a child, call 911, push hard and fast in the center of the chest. After 30 compressions, give two rescue Repeat until help arrives.

If an AED is available, follow the prompts to provide a shock to try to restore a normal heart rhythm.

Be ready to save a life. Find a CPR class at https://www.heart.org/nation.
transcript: Products are shown for demonstration  purposes only. The American Heart Association does not endorse or recommend  any specific manufacturer or products. If you see an infant or child suddenly collapse  it is important to act fast. Helping to save a life is easier than you might think. Child CPR  is similar to adult CPR but it is especially important to give breaths to a child who  needs CPR. A child in cardiac arrest who is unresponsive and not breathing normally  will not survive without CPR. Your actions can help increase their chances of surviving  if you're alone. CPR on infants and children should always include breaths done in cycles of 30  compressions followed by two breaths. First check to make sure the scene is safe. If you're near  anything that can hurt you or the child move to a safe place. Next tap the child's shoulders and  shout are you OK. If the child is unresponsive shout for help. Point to someone and ask them to  call 911 and get an AED or call 911 yourself and put your phone on speaker mode so the operator  can help you. Now check for breathing scan the chest for 5 to 10 seconds looking for it to rise  and fall. If the child is not breathing normally immediately start CPR. With the child flat on  their back kneel beside them and lean directly over their chest. Place the heel of one hand or  two hands one on top of the other in the center of the chest. Then push hard and fast in the  center of the chest giving 30 compressions. It is important to keep a steady beat of 100 to 120  compressions per minute, which is about the same tempo as the song “Baby Shark” or the rate  of the music that you are hearing right now. Push down about 2 inches, about the height of  a credit card, letting the chest return to its normal position between compressions. Now after 30  compressions you'll give two breaths one after the other that makes the chest rise. Put one hand on  the forehead and the fingers of your other hand under the chin. Tilt the head back slightly and  lift the chin to open the airway. Pinch the nose, take a normal breath and cover the mouth with  your mouth, giving one breath for 1 second while watching for chest rise. Give another breath.  Don't stop compressions for more than 10 seconds to give breaths. Continue giving cycles of 30  compressions and two breaths until help arrives. [Music] Hopefully you never have to perform  CPR on a child. When possible use an AED - automated external defibrillator -  in your life-saving efforts. When the AED arrives use it immediately. Once the AED has  arrived place the child face-up on a firm, flat surface and follow the prompts of the AED.  Try not to interrupt compressions for more than 10 seconds. [Music] Turn the AED on and follow the prompts, which  will tell you everything you need to do. You must remove clothes and anything else that covers  the chest as AED pads must be placed directly on bare skin. If necessary wipe the chest dry.  Place pads on the chest. Use the smaller child pads if they are available. If child pads are not  available use the larger adult pads. Peel away the backing from the pads. Follow the pictures on  the pads attach them to the child's bare chest. Ensure there is nothing between the pad and the  child's bare skin. Plug the pads connected into the AED if necessary. Follow the prompts and let  the AED analyze the heart's rhythm. Make sure no one is touching the child and loudly state CLEAR.  The AED will analyze the heart rhythm. If the AED says that a shock is not needed, resume CPR. If  the AED advises a shock is needed make sure no one is touching the child and loudly state CLEAR.  Push the shock button to deliver the shock and immediately resume CPR with 30 chest compressions  and two breaths. Most AEDs will prompt you to analyze the rhythm again after about 2 minutes  of CPR. Keep doing cycles of 30 compression in two breaths and continue following the AED prompts  until the child begins to respond or help arrives. Hopefully you will never have to use CPR on a  child but know that CPR combined with using an AED provides the best chance of saving a life.  If possible use an AED every time you provide CPR. Again, if you see a child suddenly  collapse don't be afraid to start CPR. Your actions can help save a life.  To learn more visit heart.org/nation.

title: Help! Is Your Baby Choking on Milk – Here’s What to Know as a New Parent
description:
It can be alarming to see your baby cough, gag, or appear to choke while feeding. Whether you are breastfeeding or bottle feeding, occasional choking on milk is a common concern for many parents, especially during the first few months of life.

In most cases, what looks like choking is actually your baby’s protective reflex kicking in. Babies have immature swallowing coordination in the early weeks, and sometimes milk flows faster than they can manage. This can lead to coughing, sputtering, or milk coming out of the nose or mouth. While it can look scary, it is often harmless and resolves on its own.

That said, frequent choking or difficulty during feeding should not be ignored. It may be linked to issues like overactive letdown in breastfeeding, nipple flow being too fast in bottles, or even underlying conditions such as reflux or laryngomalacia. Identifying the cause can help you take the right steps to make feeding safer and more comfortable for your baby.

Here are a few things parents can watch for:

Coughing or gagging during feeds

Milk leaking from the nose

Difficulty breathing or turning red while feeding

Gasping or signs of distress after swallowing

If your baby regularly struggles with milk intake, seems to be in discomfort, or is not gaining weight as expected, it is best to consult a pediatrician or lactation consultant. They can help assess feeding technique, positioning, and feeding tools to prevent recurring episodes.

Always keep your baby upright during and after feeding, burp frequently, and never leave a feeding baby unattended. Recognizing the difference between normal reflexes and true choking is key to responding calmly and appropriately.

Your baby’s safety during feeding is a top priority. Being informed and prepared can make a world of difference in managing these common but stressful moments.

description:
If a baby is choking, they won’t be able to cry, cough or breathe. Here's what you need to do if a baby is choking...

To find out how to help a baby who is choking, follow the steps in this video, or if you would like to view our Paediatric First Aid Refresher Training in full and try it for free, then get started with a free no obligation trial today! 
https://www.ihasco.co.uk/courses/detail/paediatric-first-aid-refresher-training

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
VIDEO TRANSCRIPT:

If a  baby is choking, they won’t be able to cry, cough or breathe. This is what to do if a baby is choking:
• Hold them face down on your thigh with their head downwards.
• Support their head with your hand.
• Hit them firmly on their back between their shoulder blades. These are called back blows. 
• Do this 5 times.
• Check if anything’s come out. If this has worked, the obstruction should have come out.
• If it hasn’t worked, turn the baby over so they are face up.
• Put two fingers in the middle of their chest – in line with their nipples.
• Push sharply down 5 times – this is called a chest thrust. The aim is to squeeze the air out of the baby’s lungs to dislodge the obstruction.
• Check their mouth to see if it’s worked.
• If it hasn’t worked call the emergency services.

While waiting for help to arrive keep repeating the cycle of 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts until help comes or the obstruction comes out. If the baby loses consciousness or become unresponsive at any stage, check their airway and give them CPR if they stop breathing.

title: Using An AED On A Child
description:
---

👶 How to Use an AED on a Child | CPR & Defibrillator Guide
Early defibrillation can save a child’s life during sudden cardiac arrest.

🚨 Steps to Follow:
✓ Ensure the area is safe
✓ Check for response – tap and shout
✓ If not breathing normally, call 999 or 112 and get an AED
✓ Give 5 rescue breaths, then 30 chest compressions
✓ Continue with 30 compressions and 2 breaths until the AED arrives

⚡ Using the AED:
✓ Turn it on and follow voice prompts
✓ Use child mode or paediatric pads if available
✓ If not, use adult pads – one on the chest, one on the back
✓ Do not touch the child while the AED analyses the heart
✓ If shock advised, make sure no one is touching the child and press the shock button (or the AED will deliver the shock automatically if it's a fully automatic model)

❤️ After the Shock:
✓ Resume CPR immediately
✓ Follow the AED instructions
✓ Only stop if the child starts breathing, help arrives, or you're told to stop

✅ AEDs are safe, simple and require no training. Act fast. Stay calm. Save a life.

Difficulty in breathing is very common in all trimesters of pregnancy 
1.In first trimester it is due to the high progesterone levels 
Due to high progesterone levels many patients in early pregnancy face difficulty in breathing and with the passage of time it can be better 
2.In second trimester baby is growing and due to the growing of the uterus the distance between uterus and diaphragm,lungs becomes short that's why many patients feel breathlessness in second trimester also 
In second trimester is very important to correct the posture while sleeping.
Avoid straight posture in pregnancy. try to lay down on left lateral side because in this poster many patients feel better and the problem of breathing is very much settled at this stage due to the correction of posture 
3.In third trimester  baby is growing fastly and at this stage the distance between uterus and stomach and to the lungs is almost very little and at this stage  many patients feel discomfort and difficulty in breathing 
At this stage poster is also very important. correct your the posture of sleeping and many patients feel better 
These all conditions which are discussed earlier are normal physiological changes in the pregnant lady .
But there are some reasons which can also cause breathlessness during pregnancy 
1.Anemia
low HB levels in pregnant ladies can also cause breathlessness 
2.Asthma
Bronchial asthma is also a cause of breathlessness in pregnant ladies if the breathlessness is severe then contact your doctor to treat the underlying cause 
3.High Blood pressure 
high blood pressure can also cause breathlessness

title: How to Do Rescue Breaths for Vocal Cord Attacks | Nemours Children's Health
description:
Nemours Speech Pathologists Show How to Do Rescue Breaths for Vocal Cord Attacks
Teaching the “Rescue Breath”

• When you are experiencing a vocal fold attack, the vocal folds squeeze together, much like a cramp or a “charley horse.” This makes it difficult to breathe because the airway is being slightly closed off. 
• When you take a rescue breath, try to focus on the exhale. You may feel like you need to take a deep breath in, but try not to because that can cause stridor and increased tightness. Concentrate on the exhale.
• Let’s begin with a long exhale through pursed lips or “kissy face” lips. 
o Pursed lips are important because they help shape the vocal folds into a relaxed or open position. Then we will take two short sniffs in through the nose. 
• During a vocal fold attach, you should repeat this type of breathing several times until your breathing improves. 
• Some kids find it helpful to count the breaths. 
o Slowly breathe out for a count of 4 and then breathe in through the nose for a count of 2.
• You can use this breathing whenever you need it – like when climbing steps, running sprints, or even when completing a 5k!

title: Top Choking Hazards Seen in the ER
description:
Choking hazards are a big concern for parents and pediatricians alike. Some of the most common food hazards include raw vegetables, peanuts or other nuts, whole grapes, and hotdogs. Popcorn, gum, hard candy, and chunks of meat or cheese can also cause choking. While food is naturally responsible for many of the choking incidents we see, there are other items that can pose risks. These items include coins, small toys and balls, and batteries. Batteries in particular can generate enough to charge to cause issues right away, even if the battery appears to be dead. Any of these items can cause problems if they are put into other openings, such as the ears or nose.

If you have any concerns about your child swallowing a foreign object or putting something up their nose or in their ears, or any other concerns about choking, you should always feel free to call your pediatrician or bring your child into the emergency room. title: In Hospital Paediatric Basic Life Support Infant CPR V2
How to Help a Choking Infant   #FirstAid #CPR
description:
Steps to take if your baby is choking

Things can happen very quickly in emergencies, so we’ve kept our descriptions clear and to the point.

Step 1: Verify that your baby is actually choking
Your baby may be coughing or gagging. This can sound and look scary, but if they’re making noise and able to take breaths, they’re likely not choking.

Choking is when a baby is unable to cry or cough. They also won’t be able to make any noise or breathe because their airway is completely obstructed.

Step 2: Call 911
Ideally, you can have a friend or family member call 911 or local emergency services while you take care of your baby.

Step 3: Place your baby face down on your forearm
Use your thigh for support. With the heel of your free hand, deliver five blows to the area between their shoulder blades. These blows should be both quick and strong to be effective.

This action creates vibrations and pressure in your baby’s airway that will hopefully force the object out.

Step 4: Turn baby over onto their back
Rest your baby on your thigh, keeping their head lower than their chest. With your index and middle fingers, find your baby’s breastbone (between and slightly below the nipples). Press down five times with enough pressure to press the chest down about one-third.

This action helps to push air from the lungs into the airway to potentially force the object out.

Step 5: Repeat
If the object still hasn’t dislodged, return to back blows following the same instructions above. Then repeat the chest thrusts. Again, tell the 911 operator immediately if your baby loses consciousness.

Chapter 3, Part 4 continues with the coverage of BLS. The information provided is specific to one-rescuer situations involving infants. There are a number of appropriate actions to take depending on the state of the infant, which is explained in detail during the lesson.

"If you are alone with an infant, shake their shoulders and talk loudly to them to determine if they are responsive.

Then, assess their breathing. 

If the infant does not respond and is not breathing (or is only gasping for air), then yell for help. If someone responds, send them to call 911 and get an AED (if you are not in a health care facility), or activate emergency response system and get a defibrillator (if you are in a health care facility). 

Feel for the infant’s brachial pulse for no more than 10 seconds.

If you cannot feel a pulse, or if you are unsure that you feel a pulse, begin CPR by doing 30 compressions followed by two breaths. If you can feel a pulse but the pulse rate is less than 60 beats per minute, begin CPR. This rate is too slow for a child.

To perform CPR on an infant, make sure the infant is face up on a hard surface. Using two fingers, perform chest compressions in the center of the infant’s chest. Be sure not to press on the end of the sternum as this can cause injury to the infant. (Compression depth should be 1.5 inches, that is 4 cm, and the compression rate should be at least 100 to 120 per minute.)

After doing CPR for about two minutes, which is usually five cycles of 30 compressions and two breaths, if help has not arrived, activate emergency response system while staying with the infant. The AHA emphasizes to use speaker-equipped cell phones that are available everywhere now. 

Get an AED or defibrillator if you know where one is. Use the AED or the defibrillator while continuing CPR until more help arrives or until infant’s condition normalizes. "

Pediatric Cardioversion and Defibrillation (APLS):
An Automated External Defibrillator (AED) can be used on children and infants if indicated. 
Pediatric pads should be used if the child is less than eight years old or less than 25 kilograms. 
Adult pads can be used for children eight years and older.
Standard adult pads may be used for children if pediatric pads are not available. 
Some AEDs have a switch that can be set to deliver a pediatric shock. 
If available, turn the switch on when using on children younger than eight years old. 
If the AED cannot deliver a pediatric shock, an adult shock should be given.
For infants less than 1 year old, a manual defibrillator should be used if available. 
If a manual defibrillator is not available, an AED may be used. 
For synchronized cardioversion, begin with an electrical dose of 0.5 to 1 J/kg of the child's body weight. If ineffective, increase the energy level to 2 J/kg. For defibrillation (cardiac arrest with a shockable rhythm), first shock should be given at 2 J/kg and the second shock should be given at 4 J/kg.

title: Foreign Body Aspiration in Children | Dr. Anil Kumar Sapare
description:
Foreign body aspiration (FBA) is a serious and potentially life-threatening event that commonly occurs in children, especially those younger than 2 years. Children are naturally curious, often placing objects in their mouths, which can lead to choking on food, small toys, or household items. Among the most common choking hazards are peanuts, walnuts, and other small nuts, which can cause a sudden blockage in the airways.

If your child suddenly starts coughing intensely, struggles to breathe, or shows signs of distress after choking on an object, it may be a case of foreign body aspiration. The symptoms might include a persistent cough, wheezing, or even difficulty breathing. In some cases, the child may not show any immediate symptoms but could develop severe respiratory issues later on, making it crucial to act swiftly.

Dr. Anil Kumar Sapare, a Consultant in Paediatrics and Pulmonology at Narayana Health City, Bangalore, sheds light on the importance of recognizing the signs of foreign body aspiration in children. He discusses the potential risks, how to identify symptoms, and the necessary steps to take in an emergency situation. Dr. Sapare also emphasizes preventive measures, including keeping small objects and food items out of reach and encouraging children to eat safely.

If you suspect your child has inhaled a foreign object, immediate medical intervention is crucial. Foreign body aspiration can lead to airway obstruction, infection, or even long-term damage if not properly addressed. Timely diagnosis and treatment can prevent complications and ensure a full recovery.

In this video, Dr. Sapare provides expert guidance on how to handle such emergencies and offers advice on minimizing risks in everyday life. He also explains when to seek medical help, how healthcare providers diagnose FBA, and what treatments are available, including endoscopic removal and other procedures.

Steps to Take in Case of Foreign Body Aspiration:
Assess the Situation: If your child is choking, first try to assess whether the child can cough or breathe. If the child cannot cough, speak, or breathe, it may be a serious obstruction.
Perform First Aid: If the child is unable to clear the airway, perform the Heimlich maneuver (abdominal thrusts) or back blows depending on the age and condition of the child.
Call Emergency Services: If the choking persists or the child shows signs of severe difficulty breathing, call emergency services immediately.
Seek Medical Attention: Even if the child seems fine after the choking episode, it's important to consult a doctor for a thorough examination, as some objects can remain in the airways or cause delayed symptoms.
Preventing Foreign Body Aspiration:
Supervise young children closely: Always monitor young children while eating or playing.
Keep choking hazards out of reach: Avoid giving small objects like nuts, seeds, and toys with small parts to young children.
Teach safe eating habits: Encourage your child to chew food thoroughly and avoid talking or laughing while eating.
Use childproofing methods: Ensure that hazardous items are stored securely, especially in the kitchen, living room, or play areas.
Conclusion:
Foreign body aspiration is a preventable condition, but when it does occur, quick thinking and proper medical attention can save lives. Parents should be aware of the risks, learn how to respond to an emergency, and ensure their child's safety by following best practices for accident prevention.
